content_en:
# Introducing Claude Duet

A research preview is available by waitlist today, starting with US Pro and Max subscribers.

Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track.

It’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. For this research preview, Claude Duet is included in Pro and Max plans and uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. To get access, join the waitlist (opens in new tab).

## Put your attention where it matters most

We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before.

What makes Claude Duet so helpful is its judgment. We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5 (opens in new tab) and built it to be resourceful and to decide what needs you, what can wait, and when to check with you first.

Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.

## Safety and discretion are built in

Claude Duet draws on years of security, safety, and privacy work on agents, both our own and the infrastructure businesses use to run theirs:

- Claude Duet draws on our framework for trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which also guides agents like Claude Code and Claude in Chrome.
- Claude Duet’s handling of credentials follows the design we use for Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), so it never directly sees your passwords or sign-in tokens.
- Actions are approved by our auto mode classifier (opens in new tab), the same safeguard that protects Claude and Claude Code from taking steps you didn’t ask for.
- Claude Duet’s defenses against hidden instructions and prompt injection come from our browser-use research (opens in new tab), and our models and safeguards also cover this more broadly.
- We run adversarial tests for Claude Duet’s security infrastructure. Red teams and an external firm penetration tested Claude Duet, and it’s covered by our public bug bounty program (opens in new tab).

**How Duet handles sensitive information.** We’re also releasing Claude Duet with a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt that checks each message and guards against leaks of sensitive information. An agent that reads email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where information should go. This new classifier and prompt are designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health or personal finances, are let through only when you’ve explicitly instructed Claude Duet to send it.

We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections, and will share more details about how Claude Duet is designed for safety in the coming days.

## How testers are using Claude Duet

People at Anthropic have been using Claude Duet to accomplish more, but also to leave more room for thinking and being present. Boris Cherny, who leads our Claude Code team, talks through his mental to-do list with Claude Duet on walks, instead of saving the work for his desk. Chelsea Larsson, who leads our model and product behavior design team, hands Claude Duet her to-do list before leaving to be with her kids and it saves the results for an evening report. And the team behind Claude Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews, partner with him on prototypes, and even ship code.

We gave small business owners and entrepreneurs early access to Claude Duet, and some have been using it to help run their businesses. Here’s what some of them said:

Jess gets a rundown from Claude Duet each morning. One day, without being asked, it flagged a property showing that was on her calendar for the wrong day. “\[This is\] exactly the kind of thing I want caught without having to ask,” she said.


Amin owns Shahs of Kabob in South Florida with about 110 employees. He’s used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support, and marketing, and has worked through his invoices store by store. “It brings it all together,” he said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.”


Mya had a call coming up with a potential client. Claude Duet saw it on her calendar and prepared a brief. It also noticed the call fell right before her flight and offered to move it. “I didn’t realize that it was right before my flight,” she said. “I love that proactivity.”


## How Claude Duet works

**Your context from Claude is the foundation.** Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work. What changes is how you work together: Claude Duet comes to you first, and you can message it through typing or voice in one ongoing thread, so a quick reply and a weeklong project both start in the same place.

**Work continues when you step away.** Claude Duet has a virtual machine with its own browser, so it doesn’t require your laptop or phone to be on. Describe a task in a short message, and it works out which apps to use and what steps to take in the background. You’ll receive a notification when the task is complete or needs your review.

**Receive a message when something needs you.** Claude Duet checks your connected accounts every few hours, because checking nonstop would use up your plan’s limits much faster. We’re continuing to test its judgment about when to message you, and we’ll keep tuning it based on what testers tell us. You can also tell it what you want to hear about and how often.

**Important decisions stay with you.** Claude Duet reads, drafts, and prepares work on its own. But before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your approval. A few things are off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities or moving money between accounts. You’re also able to disconnect any app Claude Duet has access to.

**Connect with the tools your business runs on.** Claude Duet can use the over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace (opens in new tab) to:

- Find the Gmail and Slack messages you’ve missed and help you reply.
- Check Intuit QuickBooks or Stripe for unpaid invoices and draft reminders.
- Prepare and run payroll in Gusto, with hours, bonuses, and reimbursements filled in.
- Draft a job posting and, once you edit and approve, post it to LinkedIn.
- Help prepare agreements and send them for review and signature through Docusign.
- Draft follow-up emails using the contact and deal history in HubSpot.
- Turn your product launch into a social campaign in Canva.
- Set up, design, and manage your Shopify store. Coming soon, a richer visual editor will let you design your storefront and preview it before anything goes live.

You can also use Claude Duet to purchase things for your business using Link, Stripe’s digital wallet. Claude Duet confirms the item with you, and Link asks you to approve the spend. content_en:
# Terminal X matches senior investor judgment 88.6% with GPT‑6.1

Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades outputs against a 54-criterion rubric, catching 25% more deviances from a fund’s mandate with GPT‑6.1 Sol.

25%

Higher detection rate when agent answers fall outside a fund’s mandate on GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. next-best model

$2.4M

Annualized savings for one customer on due diligence and investment workflows

+220bps

Higher agent agreement with human reviewers on GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. next-best model

30%

Lower cost per query with GPT‑6.1 Sol vs. next-best model

An investment firm’s edge is built deal by deal, but the judgment behind each decision usually lives in the heads of a few senior investors. When they leave, the firm takes on what <u>Terminal X</u>(opens in a new window) calls memory debt: the firm may keep the documents, but it loses the reasoning.

Terminal X’s Capital Memory operating system is designed to pay that debt down. The company’s forward-deployed engineers, former finance and investment professionals at JPMorgan and Blackstone, sit with each customer’s investment teams, design the firm’s agentic architecture, and encode how the firm invests into agents the firm owns, deployed on-premise or in its own cloud.

OpenAI models, including GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna, handle the reasoning inside those agents. And Terminal X’s Eval Agent grades the agents’ output against the firm’s standards. GPT‑6.1 Sol helped the Eval Agent catch about 25% more recommendations that strayed from a fund’s mandate and ran the same workflows at approximately 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model.

“GPT-6.1 Sol’s long-context reasoning and token efficiency allow us to build deeper evaluation pipelines. This helps our Eval Agents make investment judgment measurable and auditable.”

For each customer, Terminal X builds agents designed to invest the way the firm’s best investors do. Terminal X engineers spend weeks onsite with the customer, reverse-engineering the firm’s trusted memos and capturing processes that were never written down, such as how the credit desk screens a borrower or which sources the co-investment team pulls before a memo.

Next, those processes are encoded in hundreds of agents, customized by asset class and strategy, with sub-agents for each investment stage. GPT‑6.1 Sol handles the stages that require judgment and a huge context window: synthesizing the investment thesis, identifying key considerations, and assessing fit with the firm’s mandate. GPT‑6 Luna runs the high-volume steps where token efficiency matters more than depth.

The agents work inside each firm’s private data room, a dedicated environment for enterprises to share and manage sensitive investment data. The agents process documents in English, Korean, Japanese, and Chinese, and store what they learn as a firm Memory: a versioned record of how one desk makes one kind of decision, including its past analyses, committee decisions, workflow instructions, and house views.

Engineers turn each Memory into a repeatable workflow on Terminal X’s platform, where every production query is auditable with its full trail: the steps taken, sources retrieved, model used, and the reasoning.

According to Terminal X, customers see significant savings as a result of this approach, including one private equity firm that reported $2.4 million in annualized savings from automated due diligence and investment memo workflows.

To check agents’ answers against the firm’s own standard, Terminal X built an Eval Agent. It’s an orchestrated workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol and other OpenAI models designed to read every agent output the way a VP reads an analyst’s work.

The Eval Agent checks each output against a 54-criterion rubric. It asks: Are the numbers, comps, consensus figures, and quotes pulled from the right sources? Does the narrative hold? Does the recommendation tie to the house view?

Each check scores pass or fail. Every fail includes a one-line reason and a better source or corrected text and becomes a Memory. For example, a missed source, a wrong comparable, or a thesis that drifts from the house view is encoded as a new workflow instruction or a new test case for that desk.

“Every answer gets eval’d, and whatever the analyst corrects teaches the system a little more about how that firm works,” says Ken Lee, Co-Founder and CTO of Terminal X. “So the longer a firm uses it, the more it thinks like their own team.”

Terminal X picks models based on its own evaluation results. Across 500 scored judgments, its Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol agreed with the senior human reviewer 88.6% of the time, vs. 86.4% for the next-best model, an improvement of 220 basis points.

One class of error where GPT‑6.1 Sol outperformed is style drift. For example, a buyout fund’s mandate is to find take-private candidates trading at a discount to NAV, underwrite the business, and structure the financing. When scenario models suggest a market turn, deals start recommending a distressed credit position or a rescue financing. The Eval Agent on GPT‑6.1 Sol caught about 25% more of these departures than the next-best model did.

GPT‑6.1 Sol’s token efficiency on long-context work enabled Terminal X to build a deeper review workflow within the same budget. The thesis is tested first against the fund’s mandate, then against its recent deals. Uncertain verdicts are re-run, and the agent reconciles the results before reporting.

That deeper review flagged deals that a single pass on a comparable model had waved through. GPT‑6.1 Sol also ran the same workflows at about 30% lower cost per query than the next-best model, at similar speed.

Using GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Luna, Terminal X has built 1,700 firm Memories, run more than 1 million custom workflows, and reached a weekly active user count equal to 81% of its monthly active users.

Terminal X’s next step is to extend firm Memories from desks to individuals, so that each investment professional’s standard is captured as it is practiced, not only as it is described.

For Hyun, co-founder and CEO of Terminal X, that is the point: “The firms that win the next decade will own their judgment as data. Our job is to make that judgment measurable, so it can be kept, improved, and reused.”

content_en:
# OpenAI acquires Orchestra Bio

AI-powered drug development platform accelerates progress toward new treatments.

OpenAI has acquired Orchestra Bio(opens in a new window), a platform that helps biopharma teams coordinate the complex process of drug development. We’re bringing Orchestra’s team and technology together with Rosalind, our AI models and tools for life sciences research. Our goal is to help scientists make discoveries and manage the work needed to turn them into treatments that reach patients sooner.

Developing a new medicine is extraordinarily complex, taking roughly 10 to 15 years on average from target discovery to regulatory approval in the United States. Beyond the science, teams must orchestrate programs across internal departments and external partners, often relying on disconnected systems. We’re now at an inflection point where AI can help take on these specialized tasks and complex workflows.

Rosalind brings our AI models and tools to life sciences researchers. GPT‑Rosalind helps scientists reason through questions in biology and chemistry. Rosalind Workbench connects those capabilities with scientific tools and data to help researchers analyze results and plan experiments.

Orchestra brings a team with experience across biotech, software, and AI, along with a platform built to coordinate drug development. Together, we aim to build agents that help teams connect scientific findings with the studies, decisions, and next steps needed to advance a potential medicine.

Orchestra Bio is a platform where people and AI agents work together to advance drug programs. Scientists and program leaders delegate the monitoring and tracking of studies and campaigns to agents, freeing up time to guide the work, make decisions, and address issues before they cause delays.

A problem in one part of a drug program can affect many others. A failed manufacturing batch, for example, can delay the start of a clinical trial. Orchestra’s agents help teams identify which activities and timelines are affected, gather the relevant information, and compare ways to respond. Scientists and program leaders can then use that analysis to decide what to do next.

Realizing the potential of AI in life sciences requires close collaboration with the organizations working at the forefront of drug discovery and development. Our partnership with Novo Nordisk aims to translate its scale and scientific expertise into faster R&D and commercial execution while maintaining strong governance. At Moderna, AI is helping teams translate insights from complex data into experimental workflows, with the potential to accelerate R&D.

Our vision is for AI to help scientists across the full process of discovering and developing new medicines: exploring ideas, designing experiments, interpreting results, and coordinating the work needed to advance promising treatments. Bringing Orchestra Bio together with Rosalind is a step toward that vision. Alongside researchers and our partners, we aim to make more discoveries possible and help new medicines reach patients sooner.

### Year-old AI research lab Flapping Airplanes raises $1B at a reported $6B valuation

Artificial intelligence research lab Flapping Airplanes Inc. today announced it has raised $1 billion in new funding, about a year after it was founded.

Investors valued the startup at $6 billion in the deal, Bloomberg reported. No commercial product has come out of the lab yet.

Flapping Airplanes is trying to build AI models that learn from far less data than today’s frontier systems consume. Most of its first year went into new primitives for graphics processing units. That work, according to the company’s announcement on X, enables new algorithms that could “dramatically reshape AI’s cost structure.”

The founders have built what they describe as “the world’s most complete megakernel framework.” Index Ventures Management’s post on the round says a megakernel runs an entire program on a GPU as a single kernel, so the chip stops losing time between steps. Flapping Airplanes says its framework can handle a full training run, serve inference and play a video game at the same time inside one kernel. Memory-bound inference can then overlap with compute-bound training on the same chip.

“A model that’s a million times more data efficient is probably a million times easier to put into the economy,” co-founder Asher Spector told TechCrunch. Spector holds a statistics doctorate from Stanford University.

His brother Ben Spector, the chief executive, started the student-run startup accelerator Prod while at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and is now a computer science doctoral student at Stanford. In 2024 he was lead author on ThunderKittens, an open-source toolkit for writing fast GPU kernels. Aidan Smith, the third co-founder and a Thiel Fellow, worked at Neuralink Corp. during college. Index describes a team of a couple dozen people working in person in San Francisco.

Index and Lux Capital Management co-led the Series A round. Mark Xu of Index is joining the board. Sequoia Capital Operations and GV Management Co. joined Index in the $180 million seed round in January, and both returned for this one. Kleiner Perkins Caufield & Byers, Valor Equity Partners LP, Atreides Management LP, Jump Trading Group, XTX Ventures and Nvidia Corp. also appear on the list of institutional backers the company posted on X.

Xu and Shardul Shah, also of Index, argued that demand for AI will keep outrunning the supply of compute and data. Robotics, trading and life sciences were the markets they singled out as needing more efficient AI.

By Bloomberg’s count, the valuation has roughly quadrupled in the nine months since the seed round. Investors have now put $1.18 billion into the company.

content_en:
Legal AI startup Legora announced Wednesday that it raised a $550 million Series E round, valuing it at $8.8 billion.

The company helps automate and assist with workflow tasks for legal professionals, as the industry moves beyond AI assistants to AI services that help them get work done.

The news comes just a month after Harvey, Legora’s biggest competitor, announced a $550 million raise at a $15.5 billion valuation; back in March, Harvey also said its annual recurring revenue (ARR) was more than $ 200 million.

Legora’s Series E follows the company’s April announcement of a $50 million extension of a $550 million Series D round, which valued the company at $5.6 billion. At the time, the company said its ARR had reached $100 million. That number now stands at over $200 million, the company shared on Wednesday.

Investors in the latest financing include Atreides Management, which led the round, as well as Baron Capital, Bessemer Venture Partners, General Catalyst, Menlo, and other top names. The company plans to use the fresh capital to further expand across North America.

content_en:
Daytona, a company developing cloud infrastructure for AI agents, has raised $60 million in a Series B funding round at a $1 billion valuation, bringing its total funding to $91 million. The round was led by FirstMark, with participation from Patrick Collison (Stripe), Adam D’Angelo (Quora), Brendan Foody (Mercor), Tobi Lütke (Shopify), Olivier Pomel (Datadog), Aravind Srinivas (Perplexity) and Eric Yuan (Zoom).

Other investors included Alumni Ventures, Evergreen Fund, Okta Ventures, Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next and Torch Capital. Existing investors also increased their commitments, with Pace Capital doubling its investment, Upfront Ventures tripling and E2VC quadrupling theirs.

Daytona develops cloud infrastructure that provides secure, isolated computing environments where AI agents can execute code, use software tools and perform tasks. Its platform enables AI developers and enterprises to train and evaluate models, as well as deploy and manage AI agents in production.

As AI systems increasingly move beyond answering questions to performing tasks autonomously, companies face growing infrastructure demands. Running large numbers of agents simultaneously requires computing resources that can scale according to demand while maintaining security and isolation between individual agents.

Daytona addresses these challenges by allowing companies to launch computing environments for AI agents through a single API. The platform supports Linux, Windows and macOS, with computing resources that can expand or contract depending on the requirements of each task. It also allows agents to pause, resume or explore different approaches without losing their progress.

Ivan Burazin, co-founder and CEO of Daytona, highlighted the importance of secure infrastructure as companies deploy growing numbers of AI agents. He said:

Companies are going to manage thousands of digital employees, and each one needs a safe place to fail. Daytona ensures one rule breaking agent doesn’t spill into company wide chaos.


The company provides infrastructure to Anthropic, OpenAI, NVIDIA, Cursor and Cognition, while its customer base also includes Meta, Cohere, Mercor, Handshake, Surge AI, SambaNova, Postman, Bolt.new, n8n and Clay.

Daytona reports growing adoption of its platform for AI training and evaluation, with customers including Snorkel and Trajectory using its infrastructure to reduce processing times. The company also reported a 25-fold increase in its revenue run rate between January and September.

With the new funding, Daytona plans to expand its agent cloud platform beyond its initial sandbox product, scale its computing infrastructure and grow its international team, with recruitment planned across San Francisco, Croatia and Singapore.

content_en:
# OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol and Google's Gemini 4 Argon found critical PHP flaw affecting millions of websites

**AI models from OpenAI and Google found a critical PHP vulnerability that could affect millions of websites worldwide.**

GPT-5.6 Sol tracked down the flaw as part of the Patch-the-Planet initiative, which OpenAI calls one of the "most impactful security issues in recent memory." The model spotted the vulnerabilities before attackers did, giving developers and security vendors a window to respond. A tool on GitHub now lets server operators check whether their PHP version is affected.

Security firm Wiz found the same flaws independently, using its own Wiz Atlas platform alongside Google's Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol. Gemini 4 Argon proved especially useful for finding the vulnerability, developing exploits, building attack detection, and validating the patch, according to Wiz.

## AI lowers the bar for attackers

An exploit that worked against one specific PHP installation used to require significant effort to adapt to other versions and configurations, Wiz explains. Large language models remove that barrier because they can automatically adjust exploits across different PHP versions, configurations, and memory layouts. "This significantly lowers the barrier to scaling attacks across different deployments," the firm writes, adding that "vulnerabilities that once seemed impractical to exploit become viable targets."

The fix was coordinated over two months across five phases, involving PHP developers, Wiz, Cloudflare, and US agencies including CISA and the White House. OpenAI is proposing this process as a repeatable framework for future AI-driven security discoveries.

The company expects findings on the scale of the PHP2Shell flaw to "increase sharply in the coming months," but warns that the same AI capabilities that find vulnerabilities can help attackers too. The discovery feeds into a months-long debate over AI models' offensive and defensive cybersecurity capabilities.

excerpt_en: OpenAI outlines a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders with frontier AI, stronger safeguards, modernized cybersecurity, and more resilient public institutions.
content_en:
# Democratic governance of frontier AI, part II: Empowering cyber defenders

AI is changing the speed, scale, and economics of cybersecurity. It can help defenders find and fix vulnerabilities, detect intrusions, and respond to attacks—but those same capabilities can enable malicious actors and create new risks when AI systems act beyond their intended boundaries. We are in a defender’s window: a limited opportunity to put advanced AI into defenders’ hands and strengthen protections before advanced cyber offensive capabilities become widely available.

Today, we’re publishing a blueprint for empowering cyber defenders, building on our earlier cybersecurity action plan and frontier safety blueprint(opens in a new window). Our experience with misalignment and security incidents involving our own models underscores the need for stronger safeguards and accountability across the industry. Drawing on those lessons, the blueprint puts forward concrete proposals for governments and industry in three areas:

- **Strengthening safety and security for advanced AI:** Establish clearer responsibilities for securing frontier models and agents, detecting dangerous behavior, and maintaining reliable shutdown controls for operations under each organization’s control.
- **Modernizing cybersecurity for the intelligence age:** Equip defenders with advanced tools, training, and technical support; address longstanding cybersecurity weaknesses; and invest in securing essential services and replacing outdated systems.
- **Building resilient and adaptive public institutions:** Strengthen government evaluations and independent technical assessments, establish consistent incident reporting requirements, and improve coordinated response and recovery.

AI labs have a responsibility to address the risks their systems create and help strengthen society’s defenses. Governments must also have the expertise, resources, and authority to protect the public as capabilities advance. We encourage policymakers to act now—establishing safeguards, learning from experience, and strengthening requirements as the technology evolves.

title: U.S. bans DeepSeek from government agency systems amid AI rift with China
excerpt: U.S. Department of Homeland Security has banned DeepSeek-related technology from federal civilian agency IT systems.
title_en: U.S. bans DeepSeek from government agency systems amid AI rift with China
excerpt_en: U.S. Department of Homeland Security has banned DeepSeek-related technology from federal civilian agency IT systems.
content_en:
The Trump administration banned Chinese AI startup DeepSeek from civilian U.S. government agencies, citing security concerns.

The Department of Homeland Security on Monday made public the order requiring federal civilian agencies to remove DeepSeek-related technology from their IT systems and barring them from procuring DeepSeek products and services. The ban applies to federal civilian agency IT systems, including third-party products and services developed using the company's technology.

The move comes amid intensifying geopolitical tensions between Washington and Beijing, with artificial intelligence emerging as a key battleground in the two countries' race for technological dominance.

Asked about the U.S. move by Reuters, China's foreign ministry told the news agency that it would safeguard the rights and interests of its companies.

Mao Ning, a ministry spokesperson, said that "China consistently opposes the over-generalization of national security as well as the politicization of science, technology and trade issues," the agency reported.

The order, originally issued on July 24, applies to federal civilian agencies, including the Treasury, State and Justice departments, but it excludes the Department of Defense.

Since DeepSeek burst onto the scene at the start of 2025, several U.S. government agencies have imposed various restrictions.

Congress restricted the use of DeepSeek in intelligence community systems in December 2025. Earlier that year in March, U.S. Commerce Department bureaus told staff DeepSeek was banned on government devices, Reuters reported at the time. The Defense Information Systems Agency moved to block access to DeepSeek models in January 2025, according to reports from Bloomberg.

DeepSeek's AI models "present multiple threat vectors," the latest DHS order states, citing concerns over potential access to sensitive data by Chinese authorities and potential cybersecurity vulnerabilities.

The agency also warned that using DeepSeek's AI models could result in sensitive U.S. government data being transferred to China, potentially providing intelligence on American citizens and government programs.

The models may also contain malware or other security vulnerabilities, the agency said, citing open-source research that identified multiple critical vulnerabilities in DeepSeek's iOS app.

Executive agencies can request exceptions to the order, including delays in compliance, by submitting a written justification to the DHS within 60 days of the order's issuance.

DeepSeek and China's Embassy in the U.K. did not immediately respond to CNBC's request for comment.

title: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
excerpt: Startup Recursive has released Flint, a free, laptop-sized coding model built largely by its own AI research system, as an early test of AI that improves itself.
title_en: Recursive launches Flint, a laptop coding model it says was largely built by AI
excerpt_en: Startup Recursive has released Flint, a free, laptop-sized coding model built largely by its own AI research system, as an early test of AI that improves itself.
content_en:
Recursive, an AI startup founded last year, is starting to live up to its name. The company, which is trying to build AI that can improve itself, released its first model, Flint, on Wednesday. Flint is a free coding model that can run on a laptop and was built largely with the help of AI.

Recursive’s automated research system, which it calls the Eureka Machine, helped with nearly every step of Flint’s development, the company says. That let a small team build the model from scratch in under four months.

Flint is an early public test of recursive self-improvement: the idea that AI can build better AI, which in turn builds even better AI. It’s also one of the most debated ideas in the industry. Some researchers fear that AI improving itself could slip out of human control. For now, Recursive’s version is more limited: an AI research assistant overseen by people that produced a model small enough for a laptop.

The company emerged from stealth in May with $650 million in funding at a $4.65 billion valuation, from backers including GV, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Recursive is led by CEO Richard Socher, Salesforce’s former chief scientist.

Because Flint runs on a user’s own computer rather than a company’s cloud servers, developers can use it offline, keep their code private, and avoid the usage fees that AI cloud services charge based on how much text the model processes. The model is free to download on Hugging Face, the popular site for sharing AI models, under the Apache 2.0 license, an open-source license that allows free use and modification.

Flint is a mixture-of-experts model, meaning it uses only a small slice of itself for any given task: just 2.5 billion of its 40 billion settings, known as parameters, at a time. That makes it light enough for an ordinary laptop and far smaller than Meta’s Muse Spark Open, an open model built for Macs that was released last week. Muse Spark Open uses 816 billion parameters and needs at least a terabyte of memory.

Flint is also fast. In Recursive’s tests, it generated about 131 tokens (chunks of text) per second on a MacBook Pro with Apple’s M4 Pro chip — roughly twice the 58 to 69 tokens per second that similar models managed on the same machine, including Google’s Gemma 4 and Nvidia’s Nemotron 3.5 Lightning. On Nvidia’s RTX Spark, Flint topped 150 tokens per second.

On SWE-Bench Verified, a benchmark that measures how well AI can fix real-world software bugs, Flint outperformed other models under 50 billion parameters. On Recursive’s own average across six tests, only one model, Alibaba’s Qwen3.8 27B, scored higher than Flint.

The company acknowledged that Flint would need more guidance than the big paid coding assistants, and suggested breaking large tasks into smaller steps. Still, early reviews were positive. Wired’s Will Knight used Flint on a Mac with 48GB of memory to build several small programs, including a to-do list app and a tool that scours the web for research. He found that smaller coding models often ran into errors or were slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed his coding requests every time.

The Eureka Machine comes up with ideas, runs experiments and uses the results to decide what to try next. According to the company’s launch video, it contributed to nearly every part of building Flint, from pre-training to post-training and inference.

Recursive said that Eureka’s contributions include a sparser model shape, low-bit training that shrank Flint by 71% with almost no loss in quality and custom kernels, which are specialized programs that speed up the underlying computations.

Recursive didn’t say how much time the Eureka Machine saved its researchers, but it’s not alone in leaning on AI to do research. OpenAI said last month that by mid-August, its AI agents were logging 3.1 workdays for every one worked by a human researcher.

If Recursive’s bet pays off, each new model should be able to take on longer stretches of work without human help. The company previously told TechCrunch that its $410 million compute deal with Amazon Web Services in June was “less about headcount and more about agent count.”

The longer-term goal, Socher told Wired, is for the Eureka Machine to achieve full recursive self-improvement, with humans overseeing the process and able to stop it if something goes wrong. Recursive says each new model should make the Eureka Machine a better researcher, helping it build the next one faster.

title: ‘Open your doors for AI’: German chancellor urges businesses to embrace AI as Nvidia announces new investments
excerpt: Nvidia announced planned investments in four German startups as Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged businesses to embrace AI at an industry summit in Berlin.
title_en: ‘Open your doors for AI’: German chancellor urges businesses to embrace AI as Nvidia announces new investments
excerpt_en: Nvidia announced planned investments in four German startups as Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged businesses to embrace AI at an industry summit in Berlin.
content_en:
Nvidia is increasing its investments in Europe's artificial intelligence sector, unveiling plans to back four German startups as the country pushes to strengthen its position in industrial AI.

The investments are part of the U.S. chipmaker's nearly $10 billion commitment to invest in companies, universities and research institutions across Europe, as announced at the Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin on Monday.

The four startups are Agile Robots, Avelios Medical, Mirelo and Reflex Aerospace. However, Nvidia did not disclose the size of the planned investments.

Agile Robots develops AI-powered robots for manufacturing, logistics and healthcare, while Avelios Medical builds AI-powered hospital management software. Mirelo develops AI models that generate audio for videos, while Reflex Aerospace designs and builds satellites.

The announcement comes as Germany seeks to accelerate AI adoption across its industrial sector, with Chancellor Friedrich Merz saying the country aims to become a leader in integrating AI into key sectors.

Merz, who described the technology as a major opportunity for the country's economy, named manufacturing, machinery and the automotive industry for integrating AI. He also urged Germany's small- and medium-sized businesses to capitalize on the data they already hold.

"Please open your doors for AI to make use of your data," Merz said. "This is a real secret and a real advantage for Germany to make use of all the data which is already available in our companies."

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang echoed Merz's remarks while highlighting Germany's expertise in manufacturing, mathematics and science, saying that AI would strengthen rather than replace the country's industrial capabilities.

"AI can only augment your capability, it will not replace your capability," Huang said, describing the technology as a new instrument for businesses.

Nvidia is also expanding its collaboration with the German federal government and its "Industry 4.0 Platform**,"** bringing together representatives from government, industry, research and trade associations, to accelerate the adoption of industrial AI. On Monday, the government signed a joint declaration of intent with Nvidia to advance AI models for industrial applications.

Earlier in the day, Siemens had also announced new AI solutions developed with Nvidia at its factory in Erlangen, Germany. Siemens said the technologies could reduce engineering work involved in preparing production by up to 85%, while AI-powered production planning could cut costs by as much as 20%.

Huang had also visited France last week, where he announced investments in four French startups and met with French President Emmanuel Macron to discuss AI development. The Nvidia boss is scheduled to deliver a keynote address in Berlin on Wednesday.

Meta has poured billions of dollars into the AI race as it builds (and promotes) sprawling data centers, poaches top talent from other companies like OpenAI, and builds AI models capable of rivaling those from other tech giants. The company expects capital expenditures between $135 billion and $145 billion this year, up from the previous $130 billion and $145 billion estimate.

It’s been a busy past few weeks for Meta, which launched its AI agent, Muse, in September. Like other AI agents, Muse can do things like clean out your email inbox, book restaurant reservations, and plan trips. The Muse app shot to the top of app stores shortly after its rollout, and hit 10 million downloads in the US this week. Meta also rolled out its Muse Wonder model this week.

Muse’s launch hasn’t come without some snags. Amid concerns about user privacy, a tech YouTuber reported that the agent gave out his address to a stranger on Facebook Marketplace. The company has also had to pause Muse’s conversation-sharing feature after researchers discovered chats publicly available on the web.

content_en:
### Nvidia turns the AI factory into a product, and agents into the workload

For most of the past half-decade, the narrative around Nvidia Corp. has largely centered on the graphics processing unit. The questions have been who has allocation, how much faster the next generation is and whether anyone can close the gap.

At GTC Berlin early today, Chief Executive Jensen Huang spent surprisingly little of his keynote on silicon. Instead, he argued that artificial intelligence constraints have shifted to deployment speed, power, security, and the ability to put enterprise data to work, and that Nvidia intends to have an answer for each. “We were early to observe that, in fact, AI is a manufacturing industry,” Huang told the audience. “Rather than a tool that’s used by us, it is now part of machinery, an infrastructure, factories that are producing intelligence.”

Those comments from Huang tie together most of the massive news payload from Berlin. A summary of the news includes Nvidia introducing DSX POD, a reference design for complete Vera Rubin AI factories built by partners in containers; launching the OpenShell Reference Architecture to run agents safely; expanding its Agent Toolkit with an Agent Knowledge Foundation and a new family of structured-data models called Kumo; and deepening its push into telecom with Nokia and European operators.

Individually, these are product launches. Together, they show Nvidia moving from selling the most important component in AI to selling the operating model for AI.

### Time to first token is the new metric

One of the more interesting moments in the keynote came when Huang did back-of-the-envelope math on stage. A 1-gigawatt AI factory costs about $50 billion and should generate roughly $40 billion in annual revenue. Delay it by a quarter, and about $10 billion in revenue is lost. “$10 billion worth of revenue will make anybody anxious,” he said.

That’s an interesting and correct way to think about AI infrastructure economics. The cost that keeps AI builders up at night is no longer the price of hardware; it’s the cost of hardware sitting idle while crews pull cable. A modern AI build is a construction project, with kilometers of copper and fiber assembled on site by scarce, specialized labor, especially in Europe.

DSX POD embeds that work into the factory and hides the complexity from the customer. Each pod holds seven Vera Rubin NVL72 racks, with roughly 20 kilometers of NVLink copper and 17 kilometers of scale-out networking, all cabled, plumbed, and tested before shipment. Nvidia says that deployment at a prepared site drops from six months to as little as 14 days.

The more interesting question is where this fits. DSX POD won’t replace gigawatt campuses, which still benefit from economies of scale. The sweet spot is the hundreds-of-megawatts tier, where an operator has a site and power but lacks the time or permitting runway for a full land, power, and shell build. That’s exactly where Europe’s neoclouds, sovereign AI projects and telcos operate. The 14-day figure assumes the site is ready, with delivery set for early 2027. Containers compress integration, but they don’t fix grid interconnect queues. DSX POD shifts the long pole in the tent; it doesn’t remove it.

### Power is now a design input

The DSX platform beneath the pod is where Nvidia does some of its most important engineering work, which tends to fly under the radar. Warm-water, closed-loop cooling lets operators in suitable climates skip evaporative towers, which Nvidia estimates saves 54 million liters of water per day at 2 gigawatts. DSX MaxLPS directs power to where workloads need it, and Nvidia says this delivers the same output with up to 30% less power.

The piece I’d watch most closely is DSX Flex. During the Euro 2020 match between England and Germany, millions of Britons put the kettle on at halftime, and the grid saw roughly a one-gigawatt spike. Today, when a grid operator needs a data center to back off, the process is mostly manual, often a phone call. DSX Flex automates that interaction, allowing AI factories to defer or throttle work and return capacity.

That matters because data centers that behave like flexible loads are easier to connect and more readily accepted by communities. The industry must stop treating data centers purely as consumers on the grid and start treating them as partners to grid operators. Hyperscalers are already moving in this direction; the difference is that Nvidia is trying to make it a standard.

### Agent security belongs in the infrastructure

The second half of the keynote shifted from the factory to what runs inside it, increasingly agents rather than models. Huang described an agent as consisting of five parts: the model, the harness, the sandbox, knowledge and tools. He was clear about the priority. “The agent is an autonomous system that has access to files, resources and networks, as well as tools, and we need to make sure that the privileges we provide this autonomous system are minimal and that we constantly monitor it,” he said.

Much of the AI safety debate has centered on model alignment and guardrails, assuming a well-behaved model is enough. It isn’t. No model can be trained to understand the policy requirements of every business and regulated industry. Agents are probabilistic systems that will find creative ways to solve problems, and some of those approaches will touch data or take actions no one intended. They need deterministic controls enforced outside their reach.

That’s the thesis behind the OpenShell Reference Architecture. Harnesses run on Vera CPUs, models run on Vera Rubin, and BlueField-4 with Nvidia Sentry runs as an isolated monitor between them, capable of cutting off an agent in milliseconds. Network professionals will recognize the pattern. That’s why the industry moved away from host-based security alone and shifted enforcement into the network. It also lets security teams author policies for their own country and industry, which is especially important in Europe.

As expected, the ecosystem response to align with Nvidia has been strong, with CrowdStrike Holdings Inc., Palo Alto Networks Inc., Zscaler Inc., Cisco Systems Inc. and others adding support. The question is whether OpenShell, which is open source and runs on x86 or Arm, can provide hardware-isolated enforcement without BlueField. Enterprises should distinguish the protections available through OpenShell software from the additional hardware enforcement provided by BlueField-4 and Sentry.

### Knowledge is where agents earn their keep

“What turns these agents into super agents is giving them access to your company’s knowledge,” Huang said. Enterprises hold an estimated 70% of the world’s data, and most of it hasn’t been prepared for agents. The industry’s attention has focused mostly on documents and PDFs, yet much of the business value lies in the rows and columns of enterprise resource planning, supply chain and financial systems, and language models aren’t built to reason over that data.

Historically, getting a prediction from a table meant building a custom model for a single question. Kumo is a family of predictive models that can answer many “what-if” questions against the same data. That’s the kind of capability that turns agents from chat interfaces into operational tools.

It also debunks the ridiculous “AI will kill software” narrative. “Some people said that AI is going to be the end of software, the end of tools companies,” Huang said. “It’s exactly the opposite.” I agree. Agents need simulators, solvers and databases, and the companies that own those tools become more valuable when they package them for agents.

Huang also made a bold telecom prediction. “Every single telco in the future, with 100,000 sites representing some 100 gigawatts of distributed telco base stations and data centers, will evolve into a distributed AI network,” he

title: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
excerpt: As Amazon blocks AI agents from shopping on its site, Walmart is taking the opposite approach, introducing new technology that lets AI agents make purchases on customers' behalf, with controls over spending and transaction approvals.
title_en: While Amazon blocks AI agents, Walmart rolls out the welcome mat
excerpt_en: As Amazon blocks AI agents from shopping on its site, Walmart is taking the opposite approach, introducing new technology that lets AI agents make purchases on customers' behalf, with controls over spending and transaction approvals.
content_en:
Walmart is embracing agentic commerce with the launch of its own Agent Gateway to manage transactions and other new features aimed at customers using AI agents, the retailer announced on Wednesday. The move comes shortly after Walmart’s top competitor, Amazon, began blocking AI agents from making purchases on behalf of online shoppers.

The company’s embrace of AI technology differentiates it from other online businesses, including not only Amazon but also various travel and booking sites, which have responded to the growing consumer adoption of AI agents by locking them out of their websites completely. Walmart, on the other hand, had already announced a partnership with a leading agent in the space, Meta’s Muse, and offers integrations with popular AI apps like ChatGPT, Gemini, and others.

Now, it’s expanding on those efforts with more technology to prepare for a world where AI agents become mainstream, said Walmart President and CEO John Furner, speaking at the Masters of Scale Summit in San Francisco on Wednesday. The technology will support agentic shopping from both Walmart and the company’s discount warehouse, Sam’s Club.

It starts with Walmart’s Agent Gateway, the company’s new MCP server, which is designed to help approved agents connect to Walmart over the model context protocol (MCP). The protocol, originally created by Anthropic, allows AI agents to connect to external data sources, tools, and other workflows. In this case, it lets an AI agent search across Walmart’s online inventory and make purchases on behalf of the agent’s user.

What’s more, the retailer says that its Agent Gateway will be able to help customers shop for their usual brands or items without having to share their personal information or purchase history directly with the agent.

The company has also developed new technology to differentiate an agent’s purchases from those initiated directly by the customer, and to give shoppers more control over what their agents can and cannot do.

With Agent Profiles, rolling out next month, customers will be able to authorize each AI agent they use with a dedicated profile in their account, allowing them to see the agent’s purchases separately from their own. Plus, customers will be in control of how purchases get approved by either requiring approval for each transaction or by authorizing transactions within a certain spending limit they set.

The retailer says these controls are similar to adding someone as an authorized user on your credit card, where their transactions are identified, and you can cap their spending.

The Agent Profiles will be created the first time you use a given agent to shop through the Walmart Agent Gateway, the company notes. To get started, you’ll authorize and link the Agent Profile to your Walmart account, then set your controls or spending limits. You can also delete an Agent Profile at any time. Agent support is available for anyone with a Walmart account; a Walmart+ membership is not necessary.

Alongside these technologies, Walmart is introducing special “terms” for AI agents, which specify how they must operate and what rights they have to transact on its site. Of note, Walmart says that its returns process applies, including when an agent doesn’t act as intended. That’s a customer-friendly condition that could sway consumers who were worried about being an early tester of agentic commerce, as they won’t fear ending up with products they don’t want because of a misbehaving agent.

Walmart also says that agents can’t take actions beyond what the shopper intends, can’t access the customers’ payment information, and can only access the information they need for the given task. Agents that don’t comply with the terms will be blocked from accessing Walmart’s site.

title: PHP Armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
excerpt: This is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented by AI, but is also a high risk because of AI.
title_en: PHP Armageddon: OpenAI, Google’s Wiz find ancient holes, panicking the internet
excerpt_en: This is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented by AI, but is also a high risk because of AI.
content_en:
The U.S. National Security Agency’s sent out an alarming warning on Wednesday that two critical holes had been found in PHP, with patches already issued by the PHP Foundation.

PHP is a server-side programming language so widely used for web applications that it powers roughly 70% of the websites on the internet; by some accounts, that’s more than 33 million sites. It is also used by popular content management systems like WordPress.

The NSA warned that these holes are so severe that if a website can’t be patched immediately, it should be pulled off the web until it can be. The holes allow attackers to infiltrate the server’s file system or a database that may be used by the web app.

Interestingly, these holes have been tucked away in all versions of PHP since version 5, which was released in 2004. Websites not running relatively current versions of PHP will have some updating work to do, as PHP 8.1 and older versions are no longer supported. The recommendation is to update the web server to the current version of PHP, which is 8.5.12.

So how did two such ubiquitous, decades-old flaws that affect nearly every website on the internet suddenly come to light? AI, naturally, particularly via OpenAI and Google’s Wiz.

Security testing company Calif was engaged in OpenAI’s “Patch the Planet” initiative to find flaws in open source software. Using GPT‑5.6 Sol, it found one of the flaws, OpenAI disclosed in a blog post. Separately, the Wiz team also used AI, namely its Wiz Atlas security AI agent, Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to find multiple vulnerabilities in PHP.

Both OpenAI and Wiz followed responsible security research practices and worked with PHP on patches before publicly disclosing the flaws. Then they all worked together to flesh out what they found, and test the patches, drawing in a host of others to help.

Wiz thanked Automattic, Akamai, AWS, Cloudflare, Fastly, Imperva, Microsoft, and Vercel. (While WordPress sites use PHP, WordPress has issued a statement saying that the flaw isn’t WordPress specific, and sites running its CMS must patch their servers and work with their web-hosting companies to ensure their sites are protected.)

OpenAI says that these flaws were found by researchers before hackers discovered them. So there were no reports of exploits in the wild. This is also in part because, before AI, these flaws were too hard for hackers to exploit. “With AI this is no longer a barrier. LLMs can help adapt an exploit to different PHP versions, configurations and memory layouts,” Wiz warned in its blog about the flaws.

In other words, this is the kind of security issue that was found and prevented because of AI, but is also a high risk only because of AI.

Now that the issue has been disclosed, hackers are fully in the know. The race is on for the internet to patch tens millions of websites before hackers can attack the unpatched ones. Hence the NSA’s guidance that if you can’t patch your PHP website right away, you’re better off pulling it offline until you can.

title: Blacksmith hits unicorn valuation after Sequoia leads Series C
excerpt: Blacksmith, a platform that lets companies build and test AI code more effectively, just announced a $66 million Series C round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.
title_en: Blacksmith hits unicorn valuation after Sequoia leads Series C
excerpt_en: Blacksmith, a platform that lets companies build and test AI code more effectively, just announced a $66 million Series C round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.
content_en:
Blacksmith, a platform that helps companies more efficiently build and test software, including code written by AI, announced Wednesday a $66 million Series C funding round led by Sequoia that values the company at $1 billion.

In announcing the round, Blacksmith co-founder and CEO Aditya Jayaprakash said the company was founded to make continuous integration (CI) — the process of building, testing, merging, and validating code changes — “less painful.” In a blog post, he said that “most companies are struggling to keep up with the volume of CI they need to run,” especially in an era where so much code is written by AI.

“As agents write more of the world’s software, the question that matters is whether it can be trusted,” he added.

The company also announced that its annual recurring revenue has grown 17x and that it has run over 90 million CI jobs, or individual automated code checks. Customers include Mercury and Granola.

The Series C comes just two months after its $45 million Series B, which valued the company at $550 million. A year ago, Blacksmith was valued at $60 million after raising a $10 million Series A. It has raised $125 million to date.

title_en: Anthropic in talks with neocloud Nscale over second multibillion-dollar deal, source tells CNBC
excerpt_en: Anthropic and Nscale previously inked a similar deal for a data center on the same site in the U.S.
content_en:
Anthropic is in talks with U.K. neocloud Nscale for a second multibillion-dollar deal to lease computing capacity at a site in the U.S., a person familiar with the matter told CNBC.

The agreement would cover a second 460-megawatt data center at the same West Virginia site as the first deal, the person said. The person asked not to be named because they were not authorized to discuss the talks. The deal could be worth around $45 billion, the person said.

CNBC reported the first deal in August.

Bloomberg first reported that Anthropic and Nscale were in talks over a second deal. Anthropic declined to comment. Nscale has been approached for comment.

## AI infrastructure faces headwinds

Nvidia-backed Nscale is one of several companies that have emerged in recent years to develop the infrastructure needed to power artificial intelligence. The company builds or leases data centers and sells computing capacity to hyperscalers and AI labs.

Rivals CoreWeave and Nebius have seen their shares drop 28% and 27%, respectively, in the past month, amid concerns over heavy borrowing.

Nscale has faced its own challenges. On Sunday, U.K. newspaper The Telegraph reported that Microsoft had pulled out of a deal to anchor an Nscale data center just outside London, amid delays connecting to the country's power grid.

An Nscale spokesperson told CNBC that it remained "committed" to the project and was "exploring alternative power sources for the site."

"Our relationship with Microsoft remains strong and long-term, and this unfortunate London-wide grid issue has no impact on our other contracts," the spokesperson added.

The U.K.-based company filed to go public on the New York Stock Exchange in September.

## Anthropic's computing push

Anthropic said earlier this year that growing demand for its Claude AI models and products has caused "inevitable strain" on its infrastructure.

Since then, it has announced a flurry of deals with infrastructure partners to try and increase its computing capacity, including major agreements with Advanced Micro Devices, Elon Musk's SpaceX, Google and Broadcom.

title: Former OpenAI exec has quietly built $1.5 billion startup, betting AI can revive U.S. manufacturing
excerpt: Former OpenAI executive Bob McGrew is launching Arda at a $1.5 billion.
title_en: Former OpenAI exec has quietly built $1.5 billion startup, betting AI can revive U.S. manufacturing
excerpt_en: Former OpenAI executive Bob McGrew is launching Arda at a $1.5 billion.
content_en:
OpenAI's former research chief has been quietly building a startup that aims to bring manufacturing back to the U.S. using AI.

Bob McGrew's newest company, Arda, has raised $230 million at a $1.5 billion valuation, the company told CNBC in an exclusive interview Tuesday. The round was led by Altimeter Capital, Accel and Khosla Ventures.

Arda makes AI software to help automate manufacturing. McGrew, who was also Palantir's product and engineering lead for over a decade, said Arda's AI models have already been deployed with military tech company Anduril.

"It's a user interface and an agent that does for manufacturing engineers what Claude or Cursor does for programmers," McGrew told CNBC. He pointed to the "human-intensive" nature of manufacturing, and the time it can take to adapt production to a new design for a weapon or drone.

"When a design changes, you can retrain a human in a day — but it takes three to six months in order to change the automation to reflect the new design," McGrew said. "We've built a software and AI product that basically allows manufacturing engineers to build assembly lines much faster."

McGrew joined OpenAI in 2017 and worked on the reasoning capabilities of early models before the launch of ChatGPT. He left during a 2024 wave of other high-profile exits, including chief technology officer Mira Murati and co-founder and chief scientist Ilya Sutskever.

"OpenAI is an amazing place," McGrew said. He said he remembers being in rooms with CEO Sam Altman, Dario Amodei, who left to start Anthropic, and Sutskever, "talking about what it would look like when a model could write your email for you."

McGrew stayed through the famous weekend in November 2023 when Altman was abruptly fired and then rehired. McGrew said he wanted to stay to ship OpenAI's reasoning product, which he called the "last key breakthrough left before AGI," or artificial general intelligence.

"I said, if I could just ship that, I'd be happy with my career at OpenAI, and I'd be ready to move on to something else," he said.

McGrew, who hasn't spoken publicly about Arda until this week, said the company is using a combination of its own proprietary models, open-source models and some frontier models to run the software. Arda's other co-founders include Augustus Odena, who helped start Adept and previously worked at Google and Meta, and former Palantir engineers Alex Mark and Jakob Frick.

Altimeter's Apoorv Agrawal led the recent funding round. He met McGrew when they both worked at Palantir. Manufacturing largely happens overseas, Agrawal said, but there's a market for bringing it back.

"Manufacturing globally is a $16 trillion industry. In the U.S. alone, it's $3 trillion," Agrawal said. "We think that Arda, and the vision that they've outlined, will continue to capture a significant portion of that. Yes, the price is steep today, but the long-term opportunity is very high."

McGrew said robotics is next on the product roadmap, and automating factories could help bring more manufacturing — and more jobs — to the U.S.

"If your design changes very frequently, the only place you can really build your product is in East Asia, because you need an army of human workers who can be retrained quickly, and you can't wait for automation to catch up," he said.

McGrew also highlighted the economic opportunity as the Trump administration looks to onshore manufacturing.

"No one has ever successfully built a smartphone in the U.S.," he said. "Never successfully assembled one, and so if you can build a smartphone in the U.S. that is not taking away American jobs. That is bringing American jobs."

### AI startup Firefly secures $20M to make the physical world a safer place

The digital world has already become much smarter thanks to the rise of artificial intelligence, and now a startup called Firefly Technology Inc. wants to do the same for the physical world, beginning with workplace safety.

It has just raised $20 million in funding via a Series A round to make that happen. Today’s round was led by Definition Capital, which previously funded Ramp Business Corp. and Cognition Inc., developer of the AI coding assistant Devin. It was joined by BoxGroup, making its third investment in Firefly, and Susa Ventures, which led the startup’s seed round earlier this year.

Firefly’s goal is to make the world a safer place, and it believes it can do that by extending AI into the physical world to make safety systems more intelligent. Though devices such as security cameras, radios and sensors have helped make locations such as schools, hospitals and other venues safer than they used to be, there’s still a lot of disconnect between these systems. Cameras can see what’s happening, radios can facilitate communication between security personnel and sensors can trigger alarms, but these devices all work in isolation.

What this means is that when something happens, humans still need to waste valuable time understanding the situation before they can put together a response.

Firefly co-founder and Chief Executive James Batt Buckley believes AI can help to close this gap. He says the next frontier for AI is the physical world, which he wants to become as intelligent, connected and programmable as the digital one already is. His idea is to build a single, intelligent system that spans security cameras, sensors and communications, so that AI will immediately understand what’s happening and coordinate a response the moment the alarm registers within the brains of the humans tasked with executing that response.

The startup has developed a combination of purpose-built safety hardware and emergency response management software that’s designed to plug into existing hardware such as cameras and radios. The Ember Safety Management platform works by extracting intelligence from those devices and sensors to build up a clear picture of what the situation is, so it can immediately detect an incident, provide the right context and then organize the response. Firefly has also developed specialized hardware such as wearable panic buttons and AI beacons that enable panic button triangulation and detect gunshots, as well as a network gateway to ensure those systems are always connected.

Buckley said the safety technology industry has seemingly accepted a very strange contradiction. “The more important the job, the more complicated the tools seem to become,” he said. “But we now have the technology to build something fundamentally different. We’re starting with safety because it’s a problem we know deeply, but what we’re building has the potential to transform how people interact with the physical world.”

Constellation Research analyst Holger Mueller said startups such as Firefly are a reminder that AI is going to impact a lot more than just our digital experiences. “Ultimately, AI is going to have a dramatic impact on the physical world too, with one of the first being to improve physical safety in places like schools, hospitals and other large venues,” he said.

The analyst believes AI has obvious advantages over humans when it comes to monitoring a physical area for signs of danger, because it’s always on, always focused and therefore much more vigilant than any human security guard could be. “It will provide more timely and reliable alerts to any malfeasance,” Mueller said. “As with any AI innovation, a degree of cautiousness is still needed to make sure Firefly’s systems work as intended, but any teething problems can probably be ironed out. It’s good to see the innovation helping to keep schools and the kids inside them safe.”

Firefly’s platform has already been deployed by Colorado’s largest community college, Front Range Community College, where it provides unified intelligence across three expansive campuses, helping safety teams to quickly understand emergencies and take action. The startup now wants to expand its deployments, targeting educational centers, hospitals, enterprise campuses and other locations.

Definition Capital’s Teddy Citrin said the intersection of AI and hardware means organizations now have better ways to protect their people. “Firefly is building the central nervous system for physical safety, bringing together specialized hardware, existing data and coordinated action into a single platform,” he said.
