title_en: Ganiga secures €2.5M to expand its AI-powered food waste technology
excerpt_en: Italian deeptech startupGaniga has raised €1.5 million in an equity funding round to further developits AI-powered waste management technology and support commercial expansion.The round was led by Ita...
content_en:
Italian deeptech startup Ganiga has raised €1.5 million in an equity funding round to further develop its AI-powered waste management technology and support commercial expansion. The round was led by Italian contract catering company Vivenda, with participation from London-based NextSTEP and three angel investors. Together with €1 million secured through Smart&Start Italia, an incentive programme managed by Invitalia, Ganiga's total funding has reached €2.5 million.

Founded in the province of Pisa by Nicolas Zeoli, Ganiga develops technologies combining artificial intelligence, computer vision and robotics to improve waste management and reduce food waste. The company initially focused on robotic waste sorting, developing devices that identify and separate different types of waste. It has sold more than 300 devices for use in airports, shopping centres and large businesses across Italy, Japan, Australia and other European countries.

Building on data collected through these deployments, Ganiga expanded into food waste management with HooolyFood, an AI-powered system designed to help catering operators monitor and reduce waste. Using cameras installed above waste containers, the system identifies discarded food without requiring weighing and provides data to help operators identify inefficiencies, improve purchasing and menu planning, and manage costs. Developed in less than a year, the technology is already deployed in operations serving more than 30,000 meals daily.

The company's proprietary data platform brings information from its devices into a single dashboard to analyse waste patterns, estimate costs and monitor container fill levels. Ganiga is also extending its technology to automate ingredient ordering and menu planning, while developing sensors for existing containers to monitor municipal and other waste streams.

The development comes as the European Union introduces binding targets to reduce food waste by 2030. According to Eurostat, the EU generated approximately 58 million tonnes of food waste in 2023, highlighting the need for more efficient waste management across industries, including food services.

Nicolas Zeoli, founder and CEO of Ganiga, said the investment will help scale technology already deployed in commercial settings. He added:

For a canteen, knowing which dishes are being wasted and why provides actionable data to inform purchasing, menu planning and service delivery. The new EU directive makes food waste reduction a binding target, and you cannot reduce what you do not measure.


With the new funding, Ganiga plans to expand its technical and commercial teams, further develop HooolyFood and its data platform, and increase recurring revenue. The company will initially focus on expanding within contract catering alongside Vivenda, before targeting event catering, hotels and other foodservice settings.

title: Former Google DeepMind top researcher launches London “compute-efficient” AI company
excerpt: A London-based AI company co-founded by a former Google DeepMind research lead and AlphaGo co-creator is launching today, pursuing a “compute-efficient” alternative path to Anthropic and OpenAI’s fron...
title_en: Former Google DeepMind top researcher launches London “compute-efficient” AI company
excerpt_en: A London-based AI company co-founded by a former Google DeepMind research lead and AlphaGo co-creator is launching today, pursuing a “compute-efficient” alternative path to Anthropic and OpenAI’s fron...
content_en:
A London-based AI company co-founded by a former Google DeepMind research lead and AlphaGo co-creator is launching today, pursuing a “compute-efficient” alternative path to Anthropic and OpenAI’s frontier AI models in progressing AI.

Thore Graepel, who left Google DeepMind this summer, is launching AI company Metis Reasoning, which is understood to be initially raising tens of millions of dollars, marking the latest AI company springing up out of London.

Graepel, who is a co-creator of AlphaGo, an AI programme developed by Google DeepMind which made history by defeating human players at the Chinese board game of Go, and his co-founders have put together a 12-strong team.

The team is made up of researchers, mathematicians, robotics experts and tech entrepreneurs to pursue a different approach to AI reasoning, the process whereby an AI system works through a problem, connecting information, rather than producing an answer based on learning patterns.

The launch of Metis (named after the Greek goddess of wisdom), which believes its thesis will lend itself well to industries such as robotics and engineering, comes as investors pour millions into alternative AI systems to LLMs.

Metis’s founding team is Graepel; Piers Ingram, a serial technology and biotech entrepreneur who has raised more than $350m; Michael Warren, robotics and autonomous systems expert with experience at Boeing; and David Berman, head of AI at Cambridge Consultants and a UK government and NATO AI advisor.

Metis argues that LLMs have made significant progress and can often generate fluent answers, infer meaning, follow instructions and perform some multi-step tasks. But Metis argues that LLMs have a fundamental limitation in how they reason and can be unreliable and lack an audit trail.

Metis argues that this is a barrier to wider AI adoption, saying its adoption in many industries remains constrained by the difficulty of verifying its work.

Ingram, who met Graepel at a Cambridge barbecue where they chatted about Turing machines, says: “When you think about higher-stakes cases in engineering or science, or medical or legal reasoning, the arguments that the models come up with basically can’t be trusted. I don’t think that’s a good foundation for what we want our AI to be.”

Metis’s thesis builds on Graepel's work at AlphaGo, saying that a similar architectural lesson should be applied to AI reasoning.

Metis argues its approach is more verifiable, robust and safer than current frontier models.

Asked why Anthropic and OpenAI were not pursuing a similar path to Metis, Ingram said: "I think they are thinking about it differently.”

Ingram would not comment on reports that Metis was raising tens of millions of dollars, but said: "We have been able to fund the company more than adequately to date.”

He said that Metis’s architecture was “much much more compute-efficient" than frontier models. He said: “We are very much not going in this direction of ever larger models and ever larger training budgets."

He said Metis had “achieved” some “encouraging” results in frontier reasoning problems at a fraction of the cost of frontier models.

It is unclear when Metis will publicly launch its first AI model.

Metis is joining other new London-based AI companies, including Ineffable Intelligence, founded by Graepel's former AlphaGo colleague David Silver; and Recursive Superintelligence, co-founded by high-profile German computer scientist Richard Socher.

Asked if there was any overlap between Metis and Ineffable and Recursive, Ingram said: “We obviously don’t know exactly what they are doing; they don’t know exactly what we are doing.” But added that he thought Metis’s approach was “really a very different, almost philosophical approach”.

title: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
excerpt: Meta’s board feared that its CEO’s departure could disrupt the company’s AI ambitions. A new stock agreement gives him financial incentives to stay put.
title_en: Mark Zuckerberg Agrees to Stay in California Despite Billionaires’ Tax Ballot Measure
excerpt_en: Meta’s board feared that its CEO’s departure could disrupt the company’s AI ambitions. A new stock agreement gives him financial incentives to stay put.
content_en:
Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has agreed to keep living in Silicon Valley for eight years, potentially exposing himself to billions of dollars in one-time taxes if California voters approve a contentious ballot measure next month, according to a company regulatory filing released Wednesday.

During a dinner with Meta board members on September 9, Zuckerberg informed them that he was considering leaving California because of the measure, known as Proposition 40, and that he planned to list his Palo Alto, California home for sale four days later, the 109-page filing stated. The ballot proposal, which could be subject to lawsuits even if voters approve it, calls for a one-time 5 percent tax on stock and other assets held by billionaires in the state as of January 2026.

Many wealthy individuals, including Zuckerberg, currently avoid significant tax payments by borrowing against their shares and taking low salaries—$1 annually in the Meta CEO’s case. Zuckerberg purchased a home in Florida this past February, the Wall Street Journal reported at the time.

His potential cross-country move concerned a special committee of the board, whose members included attorney Robert Kimmitt, venture capitalist Charlie Songhurst, and DoorDash CEO Tony Xu. “The special committee was mindful about the difficulties the company faced during the COVID-19 pandemic when Zuckerberg could not be physically present with the company’s management team and did not want the company to face similar challenges going forward,” according to Wednesday’s filing.

Within days of the Meta board dinner, the special committee and Zuckerberg reached an agreement that links his ability to sell special company shares to his continued residence in California. It was finalized a week ago, and on Wednesday, Meta announced the details. It plans to create a new class of shares that hold no voting power. Selling these shares could potentially help raise funds for Meta’s expensive investments into AI data centers, without diluting Zuckerberg’s existing voting control.

All existing shareholders will receive the new nonvoting shares automatically in proportion to their existing holdings. Under what Meta called a “Founder Alignment Agreement” with Zuckerberg, he can sell 20 percent of those new shares to help pay any taxes he may owe. The remaining 80 percent would be available for sale in chunks over the next eight years as long as he remains in California. Any attempt to sell them early would require offloading some of his voting shares “unless there are material unforeseen circumstances that would render it prudent or advisable for Zuckerberg to reside elsewhere.”

Notably, the agreement specifies that Zuckerberg merely has to remain wherever Meta maintains its headquarters, so it’s possible that both he and the company could move together to another state. Many California companies left for Texas, Nevada, and California in recent years. Google cofounders Sergey Brin and Larry Page are among the handful of billionaires widely believed to have exited California over the potential tax.

But with much of the most pioneering AI development happening in Silicon Valley, leaving the city of Menlo Park could be a difficult proposition for the Meta board to stomach. “The goal is to keep Zuckerberg continuing to lead the company from California and in close proximity to Meta Superintelligence Labs,” the filing stated, referring to the company unit behind its recent Muse AI models.

In the end, the exercise may have been for naught. Recent polling in California suggests that with about $129 million spent campaigning against Prop 40, it will fail to muster enough votes.

content_en:
A rush of new data centers could bring air pollution roaring back to levels not seen since the 2000s in Texas, which has become ground zero for the physical infrastructure behind generative AI.

# Data centers could erase decades of air quality gains

New research out of Texas shows how data centers are driving up pollution.

**Hell or High Water: When Disaster Hits Home**, a podcast from Vox Media and Audible Originals.

New and proposed data centers are demanding a tremendous amount of electricity. How developers and utilities meet that demand — with gas turbines or renewable energy — will determine just how dirty things will get. So far, though, things are looking grim.

Tech companies and data center developers are devising new ways to get enough electricity, including building out their own power sources. But if all planned data center projects were to plug into the electricity grid in Texas and be powered by the anticipated grid mix, soot and smog-forming pollutants would skyrocket, according to a new report from the Houston Advanced Research Center (HARC). In just five years, it would be enough pollution to wipe out decades of gains in air quality.

“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did.”

In that scenario, fine particle pollution or soot from the power sector would more than triple, reaching its highest level since 2006. Smog-forming NOx emissions would increase 136 percent, approaching pollution levels from 2004. Planet-heating carbon dioxide pollution would climb 90 percent above what they were in 2025.

That’s not set in stone, of course. HARC modeled different outcomes based on three different projections for data center energy demand. Many proposed data center projects are speculative and could fall by the wayside. And developers can limit the environmental impact of a data center by building solar and wind farms onsite.

NOx emissions could be up to 10 times lower if data centers pair grid power with renewable electricity generated onsite. But if developers decide to build gas engines on site to power their data centers as a way to avoid long wait times to connect to the grid, the opposite could also play out, resulting in the highest pollution levels possible.

Data center capacity is typically measured by how much power they draw, and Texas has become the leading data center market in this measure with 26 gigawatts of existing and under-construction capacity. Texas is also bracing for four times more proposed data center capacity running on power generated onsite than any other state, according to a separate Wood Mackenzie report published in March. And in many cases, developers are turning to less efficient gas turbine technology in order to speed construction — another trend that’s making the data center boom more polluting than it needs to be.

“There is a good chance that our children and grandchildren will breathe dirtier air than we did,” John Hall, HARC CEO, said in a press release. “The transportation sector, the state, and other stakeholders have been working for decades to successfully bring these \[emissions\] numbers down, and that progress is now at risk.”

content_en:
Walmart will soon let AI agents shop on its website for you. Next month, the retail giant will allow you to use an AI agent on the site, with systems in place to let you approve and review purchases and set spending limits.

# Walmart is inviting AI agents to shop for you

While Amazon shuts out AI agents, Walmart is letting them in.

The embrace of AI agents stands in stark contrast to Amazon, which blocked Perplexity’s shopping agent and Meta’s Muse AI assistant. But Walmart is opening its doors to AI shoppers — as long as they follow the retailer’s rules. It has outlined a set of terms for agents, saying that “agents must not take actions beyond what the shopper intends” and cannot change a customer’s payment method. Agents also can only access information needed to complete their task. Walmart says it will block agents that don’t follow these terms.

Agents will connect to new “Agent Profiles” within Walmart. By default, Walmart will require approval for all AI agent purchases, but you can also let it shop within a certain budget, such as up to $100. You’ll also be able to review your agent’s purchases separately from your own in Agent Profiles, as well as turn off the agent at any time.

The retailer has built an “Agent Gateway,” currently available in beta, that connects AI agents through the Model Context Protocol, an open standard that allows AI agents to plug into different services on the web. Walmart says this not only enables AI agents to shop without running into hiccups that they might encounter when navigating a browser, but also prevents them from accessing your shopping history and personal information.

“For example, if a customer tends to buy sourdough bread or a particular brand of milk, Walmart will help the agent find those usual items for the customer without sharing the customer’s broader shopping history with the agent,” Walmart says. The company will let users shop with AI agents on Sam’s Club as well.

Spotify says it has removed more than 50 million songs considered AI-generated slop or spam from user recommendations over the past year. That’s according to an announcement on Tuesday that says Spotify has also made changes to its recommendation system to highlight more music made by human artists.

# Spotify pulled 50 million AI slop and spam tracks from its recommendations

Spotify has also made changes to its music recommendation system to highlight songs from human artists.

“Our editors hold the same standard and don’t program content identified as slop or spam,” Spotify says. “Since we made these changes, we’ve seen a marked decrease in listener concerns about this content showing up in recommendations.”

Though Spotify has stopped short of mandating labels on all AI tracks, it launched an “AI Persona” badge for artists that use an AI identity and don’t represent a real person. It also won’t recommend music from AI personas. Other music streaming platforms are taking a tougher stance on AI music, with YouTube Music putting labels on AI songs, Deezer giving users an option to filter out AI slop, and Bandcamp banning AI music entirely.

Spotify says it uses a combination of listener engagement and feedback, upload patterns, metadata, and third-party AI detection tools to determine whether a track may be AI-generated slop. Last year, the company said it took down more than 75 million songs identified as spam. It’s also partnering with Universal Music Group and the independent music publisher Believe to launch a tool for creating AI music remixes.

### Scaled Cognition targets customer service with low-cost voice model

Scaled Cognition Inc., an artificial intelligence lab building models for enterprise customer service agents, is introducing a text-to-speech model today that it says provides more accurate pronunciation of account numbers, addresses and other details at a lower cost than competing services.

The product, called Voice, is available through an application programming interface or for self-hosted deployment. It supports more than 25 languages, voice cloning and can work with existing artificial intelligence agents, contact center platforms and older telephone systems. Voice cloning creates a digital replica of a given person’s voice.

The launch targets a gap between natural-sounding speech and AI that reliably communicates information customers need to complete transactions.

“Modern generative TTS models can sound fantastic, but they often stumble over the details that matter most in customer service, like reading back an alphanumeric confirmation code, a dollar amount or a street address,” Akshay Kannan, vice president of product management at Scaled Cognition, said in e-mailed comments.

Those difficulties become more pronounced in languages other than English, Kannan said. Scaled Cognition said Voice enables enterprises to get natural-sounding speech and accurate readings without paying premium prices.

Voice costs $9 per million characters through the hosted API or $1 per million characters for self-hosting. The latter figure excludes the infrastructure needed to operate it.

Kannan explained how the math works out to lower costs than competing providers. One graphics processing unit can handle about 32 simultaneous conversations using Voice. A redundant setup using two GPUs on standard cloud hardware costs roughly $6,000 a month and supports about 500 million characters, he said.

Including infrastructure, Kannan estimated costs at about $13 per million characters at that 500 million-character rate and less than $7 at 1.5 billion. He compared that to between $35 and $100 per million characters charged by other hosted voices, which he declined to name.

“Self-hosting gets economical faster than people expect,” he said.

### Cloud option

At low usage, the self-hosting cost can exceed Scaled Cognition’s hosted API price. “Most of the enterprises we work with already run their own infrastructure, so Voice just drops in,” Kannan said. “For teams that don’t want to manage it, we host it for them.”

The company also claims 70 milliseconds of speech-generation latency, the time from receiving text to starting speech, rather than the total time an AI system takes to understand a caller and formulate an answer.

“Even with 16 live conversations sharing a single GPU slice, typical response time stays around 80 milliseconds,” he said. “The biggest factor customers control is distance.” Running Voice in the same cloud region as the rest of a call stack adds only a millisecond or two of latency. “That’s a big reason we let enterprises self-host it right next to their agents and telephony,” Kannan said.

One of the distinctive features of Voice is its ability to interpret meaning before generating audio, the company said. For example, its Smart Pronunciation capability determines whether abbreviations refer to titles, street names or other information and how numbers should be spoken. For example, it reads “Pay 1/2 by 1/2” as “pay half by January second.”

“Voice doesn’t just read text left to right,” Kannan said. “Before it says a word, Smart Pronunciation works out what the sentence actually means, powered by the same customer-experience-tuned intelligence behind our APT model.”

APT is the company’s model for customer-service conversations and actions in enterprise systems. When the products are paired, APT supplies conversation context that can help Voice resolve ambiguities beyond an individual sentence.

Voice doesn’t require APT or another large language model to operate. “It streams audio through a standard API and is tuned for phone audio, so anything that can send text and play back speech can use it, from modern AI agents and contact center platforms to legacy \[interactive voice response systems\],” Kannan said.

That compatibility could give enterprises a way to update interactive voice response systems without replacing the underlying applications.

Scaled Cognition is also offering a blind listening test that compares Voice with other models across price ranges. Kannan said early feedback favored Voice, although the supplied materials did not provide sample sizes or detailed results.

The company, which raised $100 million in Series A funding led by Khosla Ventures LLC, is positioning speech as another component of its enterprise AI platform.

### Thought Industries’ Lens checks product knowledge for conflicts before customers see it

Customer learning software company Thought Industries Inc. today launched Lens, an artificial intelligence product that checks a business’ product knowledge for conflicts before it reaches customers.

Thought Industries Academy, its existing course software, joins Lens in a new Customer Knowledge AI Platform.

The launch is seeking to take on the problem of knowledge silos. At many companies, customer and product knowledge lives wherever the team that produced it happens to work. Because AI tools now answer queries from customers from many of those separate sources, the same question can draw two different answers. Customers who get stuck between those answers adopt less of the product, the company said.

Lens connects to the places where business already keeps that material, the help center and product documentation among them. None of it has to move. On top sits what the company calls a governed knowledge layer, where agents inside Lens look for sources that disagree. The business sets the trust rules in plain language. When a product changes, the agents work to bring the affected guidance up to date.

Customers can get answers from Lens inside the product itself or through whatever AI assistant they prefer. The agents can also complete workflows. Logged questions show businesses which parts of a product keep tripping customers up.

Checking for conflicts between sources is what Thought Industries says existing tools lack. It sees Model Context Protocol connectors and the AI built into individual systems as mostly finding information. Chief Executive Irana Wasti said search and retrieval alone do not settle which source is right.

“When every agent is working from a different version of product knowledge, they can simply spread wrong answers faster,” she said. Customers who do get what they need “use more, buy more and stay longer,” according to Wasti.

The Linux Foundation, which runs training and certification programs for open-source software, plans to use Lens. Clyde Seepersad, senior vice president and general manager of education there, said the information its users search for often sits in systems beyond the courseware. The foundation keeps control over what gets surfaced, he said, and the questions coming in should give it “a much clearer picture of what customers need.”

Thought Industries is also changing how it describes its own business. Customer and product leaders are now the stated audience, and the pitch centers on turning scattered knowledge into a competitive advantage. Academy remains the piece that runs courses, learning paths and certifications, with AI recommending what a learner should take next.

Lens is available now in beta. Thought Industries is a private equity-backed company that has sold customer training software since 2013, and Luminate Capital Partners made a strategic growth investment in it in 2019.

### AuxoAI raises over $20M to bring AI expertise to the enterprise and redesign how work gets done

AuxoAI Inc., an enterprise engineering and consulting company that helps large businesses build and deploy artificial intelligence systems, today announced it has raised $20.7 million in a Series A funding to accelerate growth and scale its enterprise AI consulting model.

The company said it has spent over three years working with Global 2000 enterprises and strategic partners, bringing AI into the core of their operations. It focuses on combining business-process expertise, data engineering and AI agents – autonomous systems that use artificial intelligence to work with little or no human oversight, with deep insight into company data to complete long-term tasks.

AuxoAI builds AI solutions by sending on-site engineers and strategy teams to understand enterprise culture, data, workflow automation and customer engagement to tailor experiences to business and employee needs.

At the core of the company’s platform is Damia, which the company describes as an FDE Workbench, or “forward-deployed engineer” toolkit that also transforms data into applications and licenses for customers. It combines reusable agent capacities with tools for capturing a company’s business knowledge and processes.

The company said that over the years, it has learned how to work with customers to encode relevant knowledge and relationships and use that to create AI agents around the company’s processes. This preserves what the team learns in software and structured knowledge, rather than only interviews or paper documents, but in living software that can work alongside employees.

The company calls this effect “intelligence embedded in the work itself,” where consulting treats AI as a lever or tool for the customer rather than an end product.

AuxoAI partners with companies that businesses already know and trust, including Google LLC, Amazon Web Services Inc., Snowflake Inc., Databricks Inc. and Microsoft Corp., allowing the company to provide enterprise-ready AI, cloud, data and productivity via these platforms.

NTT Venture Capital, a Silicon Valley venture capital firm backed by Japanese technology conglomerate NTT Inc., led the funding round. The round also included participation from prominent industry executives and strategic investors, such as George Still Jr., partner emeritus at Norwest Venture Partners; Amit Zavery, president, chief product officer and chief operating officer at ServiceNow Inc.; and Giacomo Sonnino, managing director at Charlesbank Capital Partners and former chief operating officer of Quantum Black North America.

NTTVC’s portfolio includes Anthropic PBC, which will bring on another major artificial intelligence leader to extend AuxoAI’s capabilities.

The company said the new funding will serve to accelerate the next phase of its journey to expand its global reach. It aims to provide onsite consulting talent for enterprise AI transformation, invest in proprietary technology and AI-native delivery capabilities, and scale up its presence and strategic ecosystem.

# Cloudflare links vulnerability discovery to defense with OpenAI

Cloudflare uses OpenAI Daybreak with live traffic and security signals to investigate vulnerabilities and propose fixes for customer review.

Cloudflare operates one of the world’s largest networks and proxies roughly 20% of the web’s traffic. Organizations depend on that network to keep their applications and services secure, fast, and reliable.

Cloudflare combines OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak with its global network and threat context in Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation(opens in a new window), an early-access service offered through Cloudflare Managed Defense. The models investigate code and assess potential vulnerabilities. Cloudflare adds live traffic data, security signals, and validation to prioritize findings and prepare proposed mitigations and patches for customers to review.

Codex extends OpenAI’s role across Cloudflare’s engineering organization, where developers use it to increase output and improve code quality.

“The beauty of the automation that Daybreak and Codex provide is that you can assign machines to do the grunt work so humans can exercise their judgment on the most important engineering and security decisions.”

Security teams face a constant stream of vulnerability information and alerts. Manually sifting through that data takes time and effort, leaving teams with less capacity to investigate and address critical issues. “Traditional security teams have a ton of useful data. They just don’t have the people and time to deal with it,” Anderson says.

Cloudflare’s approach is to connect a vulnerability in source code to what is happening in production. Is the affected route active? Is it receiving suspicious traffic? Are existing security controls already protecting it? Those signals give security teams more context for deciding what to investigate first.

Through Vulnerability Discovery and Remediation(opens in a new window), Cloudflare uses OpenAI models accessed through Daybreak to investigate customer-authorized code, identify potential vulnerabilities, and check the evidence supporting each finding. The service prepares proposed code patches and, where appropriate, custom web application firewall rules to reduce exposure while developers review a fix. Cloudflare runs automated checks on these proposals, and its team reviews them before sharing them with customers.

For Cloudflare customers, the benefit is a clear path from identifying a vulnerability to protecting the affected application. The service gives them evidence to prioritize vulnerabilities, proposed edge protections to reduce exposure, and code fixes to review, while they retain control over which changes to implement.

Protecting applications also depends on the code teams write and maintain. Anderson connects Cloudflare’s use of Codex to greater developer productivity, better code quality, and fewer bugs introduced during development.

“At Cloudflare, a third of our company are software developers building services and features for our platform, and 100% of them use Codex to boost their output and deliver better code.”

Anderson describes a recent rebuild the team had postponed. “We were putting off building it because we didn’t have the manpower to do it,” he says. With Codex scaling developer productivity, the question shifts from “Can we take this on?” to “Why not?”

Anderson estimates that the work would have required months of sequencing and “maybe 10x more developers.” With Codex, a Cloudflare team of four developers took on the build. “We built it in three days, rolled it out and tested it, and spent $1,100 on tokens,” he says.

For Anderson, making AI part of everyday engineering means “rebuilding the internal process to build technology with machines in mind, not as a separate element, but as something that’s integrated into the build process.”

Cloudflare’s early-access security service puts that approach into practice by connecting code investigation with production evidence and proposed actions customers can review. The goal is to give security teams the information they need to decide which vulnerabilities to prioritize and how to protect and fix affected applications, while customers retain control over changes.

title: GM says it plans to debut OnStar AI, an in-car assistant that can execute vehicle functions and run diagnostics via voice commands, in the 2027 Cadillac Lyriq

content_en:
Americans spent about 95 billion hours behind the wheel last year, traveling something like 2.76 trillion miles. On Wednesday, General Motors executives are outlining the future of automotive at the company’s annual GM Forward event in New York City, and they say their goal isn’t to reduce that number. After all, it’s a car company.

But GM does want to make car time better. Or, as Chief Product Officer Sterling Anderson put it in an interview with WIRED, “make it more productive, make it more relaxing, make it more engaging. We’d like to make your vehicle a more central, more useful part of your life than it has been historically.” Your future car is sort of a personal assistant, and sort of a spouse, and sort of a tool, and sort of a best friend.

It’s a tall order. But in a raft of announcements this week, GM hopes to demonstrate that, armed with AI-enabled capabilities, the automaker is inching closer to that future.

GM says it will roll out a new in-car AI assistant, called OnStar AI, starting with 2027 Cadillac Lyriqs. (The name borrows from the 30-year-old roadside assistance and security service, which has 12 million subscribers.) Paired with a new app, the system will start by letting drivers, for example, turn on their air conditioning with a voice command without navigating through a menu. Eventually, though, it might coordinate kid pickups and drop-offs depending on which spouse’s car is closer, Anderson says.

GM also says it will use AI to speed up new-vehicle development, eventually cutting its four- to five-year development time in half—the speed at which Chinese carmakers create new vehicles today.

The automaker plans to expand its “eyes-off” highway driving technology to its most popular cars, inching closer to its years-old promise of making a personal self-driving car. It previously said the system was coming to the Cadillac Escalade IQ in 2028. Today, the company’s Super Cruise feature lets drivers take their hands off their steering wheels on hundreds of thousands of miles of pre-mapped highways. Reaching true autonomy will take time, but GM isn’t ready to talk about that publicly. “This industry is rife with promises that were not fulfilled. I am not keen on making them,” Anderson says.

But GM is taking a different approach from, say, Tesla. The electric carmaker sells a driver-assistance feature called “Full Self-Driving (Supervised)” that can navigate many highways and local roads but requires drivers to stay alert and ready to take over at any moment. That kind of system “presents the illusion of autonomy without its benefits,” Anderson says, who for a time led Tesla’s Autopilot program. If drivers can’t do other things while their car is doing most of the driving, it’s less useful and “comes with the direct expense of the safety of your vehicle and the people around you,” he says. “That would not be a responsible way to operate.”

GM’s method, by contrast, is to slowly expand “eyes-off” capabilities to more sorts of roads, letting drivers text or eat or watch YouTube first on some highways, and then on more highways, and then on local roads, and then maybe everywhere.

That’s when the automaker's vision gets bigger and blurrier. The cabin, the company says in a blog post, can become a space to “relax, work, and unwind. … In time, this will pave the way for a future where your car can take on everyday errands,” the company says. The personal self-driving car will pick up groceries, drop off children, and then maybe even find a parking spot at the end.

Urban planners and infrastructure experts have worried about this vision. If you lower the price of a car trip, in money and time spent driving, won’t everyone send their cars out for every task? Won’t the roads be crowded with pods full of people sleeping, emailing, and YouTubing while their vehicles slowly pilot them onward—or worse, cars with no one in them? Won’t cities become sprawlier?

Anderson says yes. If you have cheap, personal driving robots, “you will very likely incur more of those robots on the roads. And so there's a lot of societal and infrastructural considerations to make here,” he says. But he argues we have time, and that cities take time to sprawl. “I wouldn't call this an imminent thing, but it certainly is something we should be thinking about.”

title: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
excerpt: Critical PHP security flaws trigger global warnings as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond to potential cyber threats.
title_en: Critical web security flaws spark global alarm as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond
excerpt_en: Critical PHP security flaws trigger global warnings as Google, OpenAI and Amazon respond to potential cyber threats.
content_en:
The tech world is racing to implement fixes after the discovery of critical security vulnerabilities in software used to power much of the internet.

The software, known as PHP, is an open-source programming language widely used to power websites and web applications. The discovery of the flaws prompted urgent warnings from governments worldwide, while tech giants including Google, OpenAI and Amazon have been involved in efforts to uncover the vulnerabilities, detect potential attacks and protect affected systems.

The two vulnerabilities, collectively known as "PHP2Shell," could allow hackers to remotely execute malicious code on affected servers, potentially exposing sensitive data, according to cybersecurity researchers. While not every website using PHP is necessarily vulnerable, the software's widespread use has raised concerns about the potential scale of attacks.

The U.S. National Security Agency on Wednesday urged organizations using PHP to prepare security updates addressing the vulnerabilities, warning that the flaws could provide attackers with direct access to server file systems and databases. The agency recommended taking affected systems offline until the vulnerabilities are fully addressed if immediate updates are not possible.

The Federal Bureau of Investigation also warned that malicious actors could exploit the vulnerabilities to execute code remotely, putting sensitive data and networks at risk.

Cybersecurity authorities in Singapore, the United Kingdom, Australia, Canada and the European Union have issued similar alerts, underscoring concerns about the potential impact on businesses, government agencies and other organizations that rely on PHP-based systems.

Amazon said its threat intelligence team had detected attempts to exploit the vulnerabilities before they were publicly disclosed, using its MadPot threat detection system, which monitors suspicious activity across internet-facing infrastructure. It said the findings suggest malicious actors were already attempting to exploit the vulnerabilities. However, Amazon said it remains unclear how the attackers obtained information about the flaws ahead of their disclosure.

Meanwhile, Google and OpenAI highlighted the growing role of artificial intelligence in identifying and addressing cybersecurity threats. Google said its cybersecurity unit Wiz used AI models to help find and investigate the vulnerabilities, while its Gemini AI contributed to efforts to assess the flaws, test potential attacks and verify security patches.

OpenAI said researchers working with its AI models had also helped uncover critical vulnerabilities in PHP. The company said it had spent the past two months leading a coalition of software maintainers, cybersecurity researchers and security providers to coordinate fixes and prepare protective measures ahead of public disclosure.

The ChatGPT maker described the flaws as among the most significant security issues in recent memory, highlighting both the potential of advanced AI systems to identify vulnerabilities in widely used software and the risk that similar capabilities could be exploited by cybercriminals.

Cloudflare, which provides cybersecurity and website infrastructure services, said it had deployed protections against the PHP2Shell vulnerabilities through its web application firewall. The company said its measures were designed to help block malicious requests targeting affected systems, providing an additional layer of defense as organizations work to install software updates.

The PHP development team has released security fixes, with authorities urging website operators to identify affected versions and apply the updates as quickly as possible. The episode underscores how vulnerabilities in widely used software can pose risks across industries and borders, even as AI increasingly plays a role in helping security researchers uncover and address those weaknesses.

### OpenAI to make its most advanced AI models available in Google Cloud

OpenAI Group PBC today announced plans to make its latest large language models accessible in Google Cloud.

The LLMs will be available through the Alphabet Inc.’s unit Model Garden service. It provides access to more than 200 neural networks from Google, its partners and the open-source ecosystem. The lineup includes not only LLMs but also smaller, more specialized models optimized for tasks such as translation.

The first LLM OpenAI is bringing to Google Cloud is its flagship GPT-6 Astra model. The algorithm is responsible for several of the AI-produced math discoveries that the company has published in recent weeks. It also achieved a perfect score on ExploitBench, a benchmark that measures LLMs’ ability to find and exploit cybersecurity flaws.

Astra includes safety optimizations designed to make it suitable for enterprise use. According to OpenAI, the model causes “fewer misaligned outcomes” than all the other frontier models it has evaluated. It’s configured not to bypass user-defined restrictions on the tasks that it can perform.

Google Cloud customers will also receive access to GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-6 Luna, two scaled-down versions of Astra that OpenAI launched in late September. They trade off some output quality for a significant reduction in token pricing. Sol and Luna cost five and 100 times less than Astra, respectively.

“We are focused on giving customers a broad selection of models, including those from OpenAI, so they can choose the right model for any given job, helping to deliver optimal quality and lower costs,” said Google Cloud Chief Executive Thomas Kurian.

Cloud providers offer discounts to enterprises that sign long-term spending commitments. OpenAI says that Google Cloud customers can use those commitments to pay for access to its models. That removes the need for users to set up a new AI budget, which eases procurement.

Astra, Sol and Luna will become generally available in Google’s Model Garden within a few weeks. The companies plan to follow up the launch by bringing the models to the search giant’s Confidential Compute portfolio of infrastructure services.

Server-grade central processing units such as those Google uses include a security feature called TEE. The technology can encrypt a segment of the host server’s memory in a manner that only makes it accessible to a specific workload. Google’s Confidential Compute services use the technology to secure customer workloads. Additionally, they can ease use cases such as sharing a dataset among multiple organizations for AI training purposes.

OpenAI also plans to make its models available via Google’s Antigravity and Gemini Agent products. Antigravity is a vibe coding tool that uses agent ensembles to speed up software projects. Gemini Agent, in turn, is designed to automate business tasks that span multiple cloud applications.

### AI startup Vectorial lands $3M in funding to simulate human behavior for consumer research

Consumer research is a slow and cumbersome challenge that few companies do well, but if Vectorial AI Inc. is successful, they’ll never have to worry about doing it again.

The startup today said it has raised $3 million in seed funding to propel the launch of its new artificial intelligence-driven platform that simulates human behavior to generate valuable feedback for product development and marketing teams. Today’s round was jointly led by Smilegate and SenseAI Ventures, with additional funding coming from the ecosystem funds of the University of California at Berkeley and Stanford University. Angel investors from Meta Platforms Inc., Mastercard Inc. and Shopify Inc. also contributed to the round.

Vectorial believes it has identified a critical bottleneck in technology development. These days, virtually every company is using AI tools to generate massive amounts of code, accelerating the development of new software products and applications.

But consumer research is still stuck in the dark ages. Most firms still rely on outdated surveys of real audiences, which can take weeks to compile and complete, and are usually very limited in scale, with perhaps only 50 to 100 participants.

According to Vectorial co-founder and Chief Executive Taranveer Singh, many smaller startups simply avoid doing user research altogether, and just assume or hope they know what consumers actually want. But that’s hit-and-miss at best, and it leads to hours of wasted time and money spent on products no one needs.

“We believe AI is creating two distinct frontiers,” Singh told SiliconANGLE. “One focuses on reasoning and solving complex problems, while the other focuses on simulations and decoding human behavior.”

Rather than gather up real humans to test new products, Vectorial has built a platform that uses AI to simulate thousands of users within specified target demographics. It’s based on the concept of a “living model” of target customers that continuously updates itself to take into account emerging trends and behavioral shifts.

Singh says the feedback generated from these simulated audiences is extremely accurate, and he’s convinced that this method will become the standard for all new consumer products within the next four years or so. “Two pieces are missing,” he said. “The ability to simulate many scenarios, and the ability to bring your users into the same room as you build.”

Several other startups have tried to use AI to solve the consumer research conundrum before, but Singh believes that all of them have fallen short, because none of them actually models human behavior. One solution that’s been tried repeatedly is AI-moderated interviews, but these still take multiple days to organize because they’re still reliant on real humans, and they usually involve small sample sizes. Another popular approach is to use synthetic agents, but Singh says these lack grounding in real consumer behavior, which means their outputs can’t be trusted.

So how does Vectorial improve on these methods? Its solution is to embed its simulated audiences directly into companies’ development workflows, so developers receive a continuous flow of feedback that informs all of their decisions. Vectorial’s platform is powered by a behavior model called SAPIENS, which is continuously being trained on latent socio-demographic, psychographic and behavioral traits across a mammoth database of more than 2.5 million real consumers.

This makes SAPIENS 30% more accurate than general-purpose models when it comes to predicting consumer behavior, said Chief Product Officer Rahul Garg. It should get better too, for Vectorial will use the funds from today’s round to expand its behavioral dataset and build a more advanced model called SAPIENS 2.0.

“We continue to invest in our behavior model, but a model alone doesn’t solve the problem,” Garg said. “That’s why we put behavior models to work inside the product development loop. We believe this fundamentally changes how products are designed and built, because it puts users in the room where you build.”

The early results have been pretty good. Vectorial’s platform has already been put to use by e-commerce, gaming and healthcare firms such as GoodRx Inc., Boat, Everkind Inc. and Concrete Software Inc. Those customers run an average of 600 simulations per month, meaning they’re constantly getting feedback on every design change, feature implementation and so on. Vectorial has compared the findings of its simulated audiences with real user studies, and it typically achieves accuracy of around 86%.

This level of accuracy is one of the reasons why Rahul Agarwalla of SenseAI Ventures decided he had to back the startup. He said most companies struggle to understand their user’s needs, which means they’re hardly benefiting from the accelerated development times AI enables.

“Vectorial replaces the slow theater of surveys with millions of simulated humans using the product and providing insights,” he said. “This is a new class of AI designed to predict human behavior, and not just the next work like LLMs do.”

### IBM-backed llm-d framework adds controls for running AI models in-house

IBM Corp. and several other contributors to the open-source llm-d project are releasing version 1.0 of their distributed artificial intelligence inference framework, adding operational controls intended to help enterprises run large models reliably on their own infrastructure.

The release, announced ahead of the PyTorch Conference North America in San Jose today and tomorrow, focuses on managing competing workloads, maintaining service during upgrades and improving hardware efficiency as AI agents generate growing volumes of model requests.

Built for Kubernetes, llm-d coordinates model serving across computing infrastructure. IBM, its Red Hat subsidiary and Google LLC are its lead maintainers. They co-founded the project last year with CoreWeave Inc. and Nvidia Corp. Other contributors include Advanced Micro Devices Inc., Cisco Systems Inc., Hugging Face Inc., Intel Corp. and Mistral AI SAS.

The project offers organizations seeking more control over inference costs and infrastructure choices a way to reduce dependence on a single model provider, cloud or hardware platform.

“At IBM Research, we are seeing that open large language models and llm-d can greatly lower the costs of inference in computationally demanding problems such as designing hardware for quantum error correction, helping achieve a 11.8X efficiency advantage,” Ruchir Puri, IBM Research’s chief scientist, vice president of IBM’s Technology & Technical Community and IBM Fellow, wrote in e-mailed comments. “Llm-d 1.0 extends these savings by delivering the operational readiness needed for enterprises to extract more out of their computational capacity.”

The project is focused on what happens after deployment. A production inference service must handle changing traffic, hardware failures, software updates and users competing for resources while maintaining acceptable response times.

Version 1.0 adds support for quality of service across multiple tenants, zero-downtime operations and serving patterns tailored to AI agents. Flow controls and prioritization are designed to keep bursts of agent activity from overwhelming services that require fast responses, such as coding assistants used by people.

The release “adds the maturity to run it like any other critical service: a stable \[application programming interface\], multiple tenants with competing priorities sharing the same infrastructure and upgrades that don’t interrupt operations,” said Carlos Costa, distinguished engineer at IBM Research and a project co-founder and lead maintainer.

Workloads can behave differently even when they reach models through the same endpoint. An agent may issue many requests, pause to use an external tool and return for additional model calls.

The framework can keep requests directed to appropriate infrastructure across multiple turns, increasing opportunities to reuse previously processed context. That matters because agents repeatedly consult the same code, documents, instructions and conversation history while completing assignments.

A routing system directs requests toward replicas that already hold relevant cached context. Another capability moves cached information among graphics processing unit memory, CPU memory and storage, preserving reusable information when GPU capacity becomes constrained.

These techniques were previously available, but version 1.0 integrates them with operational controls, along with methods that separate prompt processing from response generation, optimize work batches and distribute large mixture-of-experts models across accelerators. IBM cited a recent agentic coding test in which the framework’s router captured 97% of available cache reuse.

In a separate demonstration, IBM and Red Hat said they ran 3,000 software-engineering agents concurrently on self-hosted infrastructure at a cost five to 10 times lower than serving the same open model through a hosted service.

The economics become more significant as agents perform multiple rounds of reasoning, tool use and revision for a single assignment, IBM said. Reprocessing identical material at each step consumes additional computing resources.

Llm-d works with inference engines including vLLM and SGLang, supplying distributed routing and operational capabilities around model servers. It is currently hosted as a sandbox project by the Cloud Native Computing Foundation.

“It delivers high-performance, distributed inference with the reliability and scale enterprises need within an operational model they already know,” said Stephen Watt, vice president in Red Hat’s chief technology officer’s office.

title: HSBC CEO warns the AI boom won’t make every data center a good bet
excerpt: Data center campuses house the servers that power AI and cloud computing.
title_en: HSBC CEO warns the AI boom won’t make every data center a good bet
excerpt_en: Data center campuses house the servers that power AI and cloud computing.
content_en:
AI is a transformational technology worth investing in — but investors must be selective when investing in data centers, according to the head of one of the world's biggest banks.

Speaking to CNBC's Dan Murphy on Tuesday, HSBC CEO Georges Elhedery called artificial intelligence "a major enabler to re-engineer and reimagine all our businesses, all our activities."

"It's going to put a lot of power back in the hands of our colleagues because of the level of productivity it gives them, so it's going to be transformational, and we're certainly very much on a journey to adopt it," he said, adding that AI would help to "re-engineer the bank."

But when it comes to investing in infrastructure underpinning the technology, he advised discernment over an all-in approach.

"One has to be selective," Elhedery said. "You have to look at the quality of the tenancy agreements. You have to look at the pricing of these contracts. Not all of them are of that level of virtuosity that you can support strongly. Some of them may be more challenging."

HSBC was ranked as the seventh-largest bank in the world and the biggest lender in Europe by S&P Global last year, with assets worth close to $3 trillion. The bank — headquartered in London — is both a financier and operator of data centers.

In its 2025 annual report, HSBC said it intends to become "the leading bank for fast-growing transition ecosystems," noting that its customer base spans areas including data centers and the AI sector.

Data center campuses house the servers that power AI and cloud computing, and have seen a multibillion-dollar boom in recent years.

Global spending on data centers could reach $7 trillion by 2030, according to McKinsey, with Big Tech increasingly tapping private credit and taking on debt to fund the development of the facilities.

But AI borrowing is becoming a source of tension in financial markets, as the cost of capital soars and corporations add to huge debt piles as they race to finance AI and the build-out of data centers.

Speaking at LSEG and Eurasia Group's GZERO Summit in London earlier this month, Mohamed El-Erian, chief economic adviser of Allianz and former CEO of PIMCO, highlighted the competition for financing between governments and AI-related companies as a source of pressure in bond markets.

"Governments are borrowing what they're borrowing, plus they're refinancing debt at a higher level of rates," he said. "\[And\] you have hyperscalers who last year raised $200 billion in bond financing, and are probably going to raise a trillion in bond financing this year. They are yield insensitive. They are spread insensitive because they are betting on something that is truly transformational."

Bond yields issued by various major economies have hit multi-decade highs in 2026, amid concerns around elevated government deficits and mounting debt levels alongside fears of sticky inflation and more hawkish central banks.

JPMorgan Chase estimated earlier this year that $4.1 trillion in AI-related debt will be issued by the end of the decade, as data center and other AI-adjacent companies splurge on building capacity.

# Anthropic takes on Grok Bot, Meta's Muse, and OpenAI's Dots with its always-on agent "Claude Duet"

## Key Points

- Anthropic has released a preview of "Claude Duet," an app where an AI agent handles tasks for the user in the background.
- The app runs on cloud computers and connects to outside services like Gmail, Slack, and Stripe. It can schedule meetings or prepare billing, among other things.
- The system always asks for the user's approval before actions like payments or sending messages. Bank transfers are blocked entirely.

**Anthropic has answered Grok Bot, Meta's Muse, and OpenAI's Dots with a research preview of Claude Duet. The standalone app runs Claude as a proactive agent that keeps working on tasks while the user is away and asks for approval before taking sensitive steps.**

Anthropic is pitching Claude Duet to professionals and small business owners who have "more on their plates than they can track." The app runs on iOS, Android, and the web at claude.ai and is built on Claude Opus 5.5. Pro and Max subscribers in the US can get access through a waitlist. Team and Enterprise plans aren't included yet.

Anthropic says the big difference from the regular Claude app is which way things flow. In the Claude app, users open a chat. Duet comes to them instead. Every morning, the agent sends a short summary of the most important items from connected apps. After that, it only reaches out when something needs attention. It pulls memory, skills, and app connections from the user's existing Claude account.

Users assign tasks by text or voice message in a single ongoing thread. According to Anthropic, that covers everything from scheduling to dashboards and financial forecasts to prototypes and web apps. The agent works on a virtual machine, its own cloud computer with a browser, so the user's laptop or phone doesn't need to stay on.

Duet connects to services like Gmail, Slack, Stripe, Docusign, and Shopify through more than 6,000 connectors and plugins from the Claude Marketplace. That lets it track down unpaid invoices and draft payment reminders, or get payroll ready. For purchases, it uses Stripe Link with a virtual card, so the user's real card number never gets shared.

Several competitors have launched similar products in recent months. SpaceXAI opened the Grok Bot beta in August. In September, Meta followed with Muse and OpenAI with its Dots. All of them are betting on personal agents that handle tasks independently and act on their own initiative.

## Users keep the final say on anything risky

Anthropic says Duet can only read, draft, and prepare on its own. Before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows exactly what it plans to do and waits for the user's approval. Trading securities and moving money between accounts are off the table, even with approval.

Technical safeguards add another layer. The company says the agent never sees passwords or login tokens directly, because credential handling follows the design of Claude Managed Agents. To fend off hidden instructions, known as prompt injections, Anthropic uses defenses from its research on browser use. Red teams and an outside firm also ran attack tests to probe Duet for weak spots.

Anthropic also built a new classifier for Duet. This screening system works with special safety instructions in the system prompt to check every message for leaking sensitive data. Together, they're meant to refuse requests to share credit card numbers or ID details. Health or personal finance information only gets through when the user explicitly says so.

## Anthropic admits Duet still misses things

Anthropic concedes that the early version can misread a message thread, misjudge urgency, and miss things that arrive between two checks. It's also weaker at personal errands like booking tickets, since its core features are built for work.

Duet only checks connected accounts every few hours, and Anthropic says that comes down to usage. Constant checking would burn through subscription limits much faster. Duet shares those limits with other Claude products, and the background checks count against them too.

Anthropic plans to use tester feedback to tune when the agent should reach out. How Duet fits with the Claude app is still an open question. For now, it runs separately, and early users' experience will shape how the two work together.

title: How AI is an inherently imperial technology, and how the US and China are building rival "AI empires" with different approaches to extend their power
excerpt: How AI is an inherently imperial technology, and how the US and China are building rival "AI empires" with different approaches to extend their power
title_en: How AI is an inherently imperial technology, and how the US and China are building rival "AI empires" with different approaches to extend their power
excerpt_en: How AI is an inherently imperial technology, and how the US and China are building rival "AI empires" with different approaches to extend their power
content_en:
In the span of a few years, China and the United States have each assembled something future historians might recognize as a new kind of empire. Their dominions extend not merely over territory, trade routes, and airspace but over knowledge itself. By controlling the large language models, chips, physical infrastructure, and capital that provide the foundations for advanced machine cognition, Beijing and Washington are not only attaining new heights of economic performance and power projection; they are also setting the terms of all future scientific and intellectual progress. The term “AI superpowers” fails to capture the influence and reach that these rivals now wield. Even without active alliance building or coercion, they can make all other countries that seek access to advanced AI beholden to them.

Imperial history carries a warning. In the absence of other forces, empires seldom succumb to a challenger or to barbarians at the gates. More often, they fail because defending their vast dominions drains them dry, whether of material resources, the consent of the governed, or the loyalty of elites. The imperial center finds it can no longer maintain control over the periphery—the regions that once submitted to it. Failure can be financial, as it was for the British Empire after 1945, when the debts of two world wars forced London to liquidate its imperial assets to pay the price of victory: a welfare state for the citizens of the imperial metropole. It can be institutional, as it was for the Qing empire in the late nineteenth century, when it failed to industrialize, reform its bureaucracy, and renew the legitimacy of the Manchu dynasty.

Or it can be technological. The Royal Navy’s *Dreadnought* of 1906 gave the United Kingdom the first “all big gun” battleship and, with the same stroke, rendered its existing battle fleet obsolete. Overnight, this breakthrough opened the way for rivals such as Germany, erasing a century of accumulated British advantage. The resulting arms race forced the United Kingdom to nearly double naval spending between 1900 and 1914 and clashed with the Liberal government’s new social spending commitments, such as the Old Age Pension Act of 1908. The decisive question in the contest between Beijing and Washington may therefore not be who achieves artificial general intelligence first, but who can bankroll the race.

AI is imperial in two ways. On the one hand, China and the United States had empire-like qualities before the AI race began: Washington, the incumbent, pairs global military primacy with an alliance system no rival can match. It also supplies the currency for the lion’s share of international trade and transactions. Beijing, often described as the challenger, combines industrial and supply chain dominance with the world’s largest navy and a tightening grip on the physical and digital infrastructure of countries across Africa, Asia, and Latin America. For both, AI is a way to extend the power they already wield. But AI is also by its nature an imperial substance. Whoever produces and controls frontier models acquires global leverage over innovation, production, science, culture, and, ultimately, advanced thought. Much as silver underwrote Habsburg Spain and oil defined the “American century,” this new commodity will not merely enrich the powers that dominate it but also provide the basic operating system on which everyone else must depend.

What distinguishes the AI empires from their forerunners is not ambition but velocity. The familiar imperial arc—expansion, overreach, strain, unraveling—once played out across a century or even a millennium. Today, that process is happening at machine speed. The question is whether the new hegemons can convert their particular endowments—the United States’ capital markets, frontier labs, and transistors and China’s state direction, cheap energy, and watts—into durable imperial orders or whether they will run aground trying.

### SUPREMACY BY SCARCITY

An empire is more than a great power. It is a polity whose authority and influence extend over vast territories and peoples without their express consent. Throughout history, empires have differed in almost every respect: in their form of government at home, in the kinds of resources they seek to control, in how their authority is sustained. They may be autocracies or republics; they may rely on soldiers and settlers or civil servants and chartered companies. Yet the underlying vector of power never changes. A center commands, and a periphery obeys. In practice, the most durable empires have relied on informal collaboration with local elites, whereas brutally coercive ones tend to be short-lived. Of course, any form of state power must not only monopolize violence but also be able to wield it. What sets empires apart is the capacity to elicit submission across immense distances. And they occur throughout history for a reason: by exploiting economies of scale, empires can achieve dominance and deliver security more efficiently than alternative structures, whether confederations or alliances of city-states. The nation-state is a relative newcomer.

Empires have often projected power through technological leadership. In antiquity, Rome’s aqueducts and China’s canals and flood-control works were the pipelines of centuries of hegemony. The imperial powers of early modern Europe led the world in printing, maritime technology, and artillery. The Cold War rivals were nuclear superpowers. Yet artificial intelligence may now give China and the United States greater imperial reach than any of those earlier technologies—and far more swiftly.

Several features mark AI as an imperial technology rather than a merely commercial one. First is the return of scarcity that it enables. An empire is, at its heart, a system for controlling finite strategic resources: able-bodied humans, arable land, grain, metals, and minerals. From the 1970s to the 2010s, software escaped this logic because it could be mass-produced at almost zero cost atop abundant, cheap silicon. AI has shattered that reprieve. According to the industry’s scaling laws, a model’s performance climbs relative to the number of parameters it contains, the volume of data it is trained on, and the processing power, or compute, spent training it. Progress therefore depends on energy, critical minerals, advanced chips, and capital on a massive scale. The moment a technology’s frontier comes to depend on vast quantities of scarce inputs, its production becomes a matter of geopolitics.

AI is by its nature an imperial technology.

AI also has an inherent center-periphery structure. Control of frontier AI and its rewards are concentrated in a handful of firms in China and the United States. Everyone else is a dependent user, whether a government running public services on a model it cannot inspect or a firm building products on an interface that can be repriced or withdrawn overnight. At the same time, AI inputs, both material and human, are drawn disproportionately from the periphery. Minerals from the Democratic Republic of the Congo and Indonesia and “ghost laborers” from Kenya and the Philippines, paid a few dollars an hour to label and filter the data from which a model in Silicon Valley learns—the plantation economics of the chatbot age. Raw inputs are extracted from the periphery, refined and assembled in the metropole, and sold back at a markup.

Like many empires, the AI stack is organized around chokepoints. Not all imperial power results from outright conquest, and not all those who are ruled are colonial subjects. The ascendancy of the British Empire in the nineteenth century was not driven primarily by vast territorial holdings, many of which had little economic value, or from control over factories and intellectual property—which was so poorly protected as to be effectively open source. Swiss robotics startup Enact Intelligence has today emerged out of stealth, with a $30m pre-seed round and backing from two heavyweights from the French AI ecosystem, Mistral boss Arthur Mensch and Meta's former AI chief scientist Yann LeCun.

The $30m funding is high for a pre-seed funding round and comes as investors continue to invest heavily in robotics. Enact is building the underlying technology for general purpose robots.

It says it’s developing tech that enables robots to manipulate objects with greater accuracy by sensing force and touch, as it looks to make robots carry out work in industrial settings and in the real world.

Its approach is different to those robotics companies which rely on cameras and visuals.

Manuel Yves Galliker, its CEO and co-founder, who previously worked at the hot US robotics startup Physical Intelligence, said: “In particular, our robots sense force and touch through their own actuators, so they feel what’s happening in real time, and learn more data-efficiently while simultaneously pushing reliability and performance. A technology that works across every form factor, built for real-world deployment from day one."

Investors in the round include Redalpine, Notion Capital and Firstminute Capital, with angel investors including Mensch, LeCun and Hugging Face’s Thomas Wolf.

The startup is using the funds to expand the team and accelerate its hardware and R&D development.

The CEO added: “We’re rethinking the full stack, from model architectures enabling multi-frequency and multi-scale intelligence, to the data pipelines all the way down to the actuators and sensors that feed the model.”

content_en:
French-American AI startup Reduck has raised $3 million in a pre-seed funding round led by Daphni, with participation from Drysdale Ventures and Galion.exe. The company is developing technology that enables AI agents to interact with websites and automate tasks without relying on traditional APIs.

Founded by Daniel Huynh (CEO), Louis Abraham (CTO) and Raphaël Millet (COO), Reduck aims to address one of the challenges limiting the adoption of AI agents: the lack of direct access to websites and business applications.

While AI agents are increasingly being developed to automate digital tasks, many websites and internal business tools do not provide APIs or Model Context Protocol (MCP) interfaces that allow agents to interact with them directly. As a result, agents often rely on browser-based interactions, such as clicking and typing, which can be slow, costly and unreliable when performing complex tasks.

To address this challenge, Reduck has developed Reduck MCP, a platform that allows AI agents to discover, execute and create browser automation scripts. Instead of navigating websites step by step, agents can use predefined scripts to complete tasks, reducing the time and computational resources required.

According to the company, its technology can make agents three times faster and cheaper across tasks such as downloading invoices from multiple vendors and conducting market research on LinkedIn. Reduck's library currently includes more than 1,200 ready-to-run automation scripts covering over 250 websites.

To expand and improve this library, Reduck is developing a system of AI agents capable of creating and maintaining automation scripts autonomously, with a focus on reliability and scalability.

Alongside these developments, the company is preparing a developer offering that will enable teams to build custom AI agent systems connected to applications without APIs, including specialised portals in insurance and healthcare and internal customer relationship management systems. Reduck is also exploring applications for automating knowledge work, starting with generative engine optimisation (GEO).

The new funding has supported the expansion of Reduck's team across AI engineering, full-stack development and infrastructure. The company plans to further improve its automation technology, expand its script library and introduce a new offering for developers.

content_en:
**Enact Intelligence**, a physical AI startup headquartered in Zurich, has come out of stealth today with a €26.68 million ($30 million) pre-Seed funding round, one of the largest pre-Seed raises in Europe to date.

The round saw participation from institutional investors redalpine, Notion Capital and firstminute capital, alongside a notable slate of angel investors, including Arthur Mensch, founder of Mistral; Yann LeCun, founder of AMI Labs and former Chief AI Scientist at Meta; and Andrew Lonsberry, founder of Path Robotics.

“*Dexterity is the next frontier in robotics, and Enact is tackling it with a new data modality: starting with high precision force data from bespoke actuators they are rethinking the entire stack from the hardware up. We are very excited about Enact’s approach of leveraging orthogonal data to improve existing models and build a data moat*,” said **Dr. Harald Nieder**, General Partner of redalpine.

Founded in March 2026 by Manuel Yves Galliker, Enact is building robots that can not only see their environment but physically sense what is happening when they interact with it. Before founding Enact, Galliker led the software team for the humanoid robot NEO at 1X, helped build 1X’s AI team in Silicon Valley, and went on to work at the robotics lab Physical Intelligence.

The central argument of Enact is that most robots today depend almost entirely on vision to perceive their surroundings, limiting their ability to manipulate objects reliably or learn efficiently from experience. Existing haptic sensing solutions, which extend robots with force and touch, are either too costly or fragile for meaningful industrial deployment.

To solve this physical AI challenge, Enact rethinks the entire stack, from model architectures and data pipelines through to the actuators and sensors that feed the model. As a departure from traditional robots relying on point-based force sensors, Enact’s robots capture force data directly from the actuators themselves, similar to how humans sense tension through their muscles rather than solely through their fingertips.

**Manuel Yves Galliker**, CEO and founder of Enact Intelligence, said, “*Unlike the early days of LLMs, physical AI has the advantage of starting from strong reasoning, language, and vision capabilities already in place. Instead of trying to collect every piece of data needed to teach a robot common sense about the world, we can build on top of existing models, like video models, and adapt them to output robot actions for interacting with the real world. So what we are addressing is the ability to efficiently learn from experience and perform tasks reliably, both of which require the model to understand the physics of the robot and the task at hand*.”

This approach, Galliker argues, will lead to the development of “a proprioceptive nerve system and the cortex that makes sense of it,” solving dexterity through whole-body force-awareness at a cost and reality-level suitable for industrial scale.

Enact’s twelve-person team draws its engineering talent from DeepMind, 1X, Amazon Robotics, Helsing, Physical Intelligence and ETH Zurich. Alongside the funding, the company announced bringing Philip Kneis, a former DeepTech investor at redalpine, to lead growth.

“*Silicon Valley has traditionally been very strong in software and AI, but it’s lacking in robotics and hardware engineering talent, and with the current excitement around robotics a lot of money is chasing a few people. What we will do is bring the AI experience with us from Silicon Valley and combine it with Zürich’s local talent pool. That’s the winning formula*,” added Galliker.

The fresh capital will be used to grow its team fivefold by the end of 2027, accelerate its hardware and R&D pipelines, and roll out its robots with multiple industrial partners across manufacturing, infrastructure, retail, and food processing.
